questions.question_text: If a straight line drawn through the point of intersection of the lines $4x+3y-1=0$ and $3x+4y-1=0$ , meets the co-ordinate axes at the points P and Q , then the locus of the mid point of PQ is :
questions.question_html: If a straight line drawn through the point of intersection of the lines $4x+3y-1=0$ and $3x+4y-1=0$ , meets the co-ordinate axes at the points P and Q , then the locus of the mid point of PQ is :
questions.explanation_text: 1. A straight line $L$ passes through the point of intersection of 2 straight lines: ${\begin{aligned} L_{1}:4x+3y-1=0 \\ L_{2}:3x+4y-1=0 \end{aligned}$ 2. The straight line $L$ cuts the axes at $P$ and $Q$ 3. To identify the locus of the mid-point of the segment $PQ$ The point of intersection of $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ is $I(𝜶,𝜷)$ The mid-point of the segment $PQ$ is $M(h,k)$ Analytical Study : We first solve the pair of straight lines $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ to locate the point of intersection : $\begin{aligned} & 4x+3y-1=0 \Rightarrow 12x+9y=3 \\ & 3x+4y-1=0 \Rightarrow 12x+16y=4 \end{aligned} \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{1}{7} \Rightarrow 𝜶=\frac{1}{7} \Rightarrow I(\frac{1}{7},\frac{1}{7})\dots..(i)$ The straight line $L$ passes through the point $I$ identified by equation (i) The equation of the straight line $L$ in point slope form is written below : $L:(y-\frac{1}{7})=m(x-\frac{1}{7}) \equiv L:7mx-7y=m-1 \equiv L:\frac{7mx}{m-1}+\frac{7y}{1-m}=1\dots.(ii)$ The equation (ii) gives the straight line $L$ in intercept form where the $X$ and $Y$ intercepts are observed below : $\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} P & Q \\ (\frac{m-1}{7m},0) & (0,\frac{1-m}{7}) \end{aligned}\text{..... Chart}1 \end{aligned}$ From Chart 1, the mid-point of the section $PQ$ is derived applying mid-point formulae : $M(ℎ,k)=M(\frac{m-1}{14m},\frac{1-m}{14}) \equiv \begin{aligned} \text{Point} & ℎ & k \\ M(ℎ,k) & \frac{m-1}{14m} & \frac{1-m}{14} \end{aligned}\dots.\text{Chart}2$ Chart 2 has the $X$ and $Y$ coordinate each as a function of $m$ where we can eliminate $m$ and mathematically trace the locus : $k=\frac{1-m}{14} \Rightarrow m=1-14k \Rightarrow h=\frac{1-14k-1}{14(1-14k)}=\frac{14k}{14(14k-1)}=\frac{k}{(14k-1)} \Rightarrow 14hk-h=k \Rightarrow h+k-14hk=0$ The locus of the mid-point of the section $PQ$ after replacement of the dummy variables is found to be the rectangular hyperbola $x+y-14xy=0$
questions.explanation_html:
1. 1. A straight line $L$ passes through the point of intersection of 2 straight lines: ${\begin{aligned} L_{1}:4x+3y-1=0 \\ L_{2}:3x+4y-1=0 \end{aligned}$

  2. 2. The straight line $L$ cuts the axes at $P$ and $Q$

  3. 3. To identify the locus of the mid-point of the segment $PQ$

  1. The point of intersection of $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ is $I(𝜶,𝜷)$

  2. The mid-point of the segment $PQ$ is $M(h,k)$

Analytical Study :

We first solve the pair of straight lines $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ to locate the point of intersection :

$\begin{aligned} & 4x+3y-1=0 \Rightarrow 12x+9y=3 \\ & 3x+4y-1=0 \Rightarrow 12x+16y=4 \end{aligned} \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{1}{7} \Rightarrow 𝜶=\frac{1}{7} \Rightarrow I(\frac{1}{7},\frac{1}{7})\dots..(i)$

The straight line $L$ passes through the point $I$ identified by equation (i)

The equation of the straight line $L$ in point slope form is written below :

$L:(y-\frac{1}{7})=m(x-\frac{1}{7}) \equiv L:7mx-7y=m-1 \equiv L:\frac{7mx}{m-1}+\frac{7y}{1-m}=1\dots.(ii)$

The equation (ii) gives the straight line $L$ in intercept form where the $X$ and $Y$ intercepts are observed below :

$\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} P & Q \\ (\frac{m-1}{7m},0) & (0,\frac{1-m}{7}) \end{aligned}\text{..... Chart}1 \end{aligned}$

From Chart 1, the mid-point of the section $PQ$ is derived applying mid-point formulae :

$M(ℎ,k)=M(\frac{m-1}{14m},\frac{1-m}{14}) \equiv \begin{aligned} \text{Point} & ℎ & k \\ M(ℎ,k) & \frac{m-1}{14m} & \frac{1-m}{14} \end{aligned}\dots.\text{Chart}2$

Chart 2 has the $X$ and $Y$ coordinate each as a function of $m$ where we can eliminate $m$ and mathematically trace the locus :

$k=\frac{1-m}{14} \Rightarrow m=1-14k \Rightarrow h=\frac{1-14k-1}{14(1-14k)}=\frac{14k}{14(14k-1)}=\frac{k}{(14k-1)} \Rightarrow 14hk-h=k \Rightarrow h+k-14hk=0$

The locus of the mid-point of the section $PQ$ after replacement of the dummy variables is found to be the rectangular hyperbola $x+y-14xy=0$

questions.question_text: Let the mid points of the sides of a triangle ABC be $(\frac{5}{2},7)$ , $(\frac{5}{2},3)$ and $(4,5)$ . If its incentre is $(ℎ,k)$ , then $3ℎ+k$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let the mid points of the sides of a triangle ABC be $(\frac{5}{2},7)$ , $(\frac{5}{2},3)$ and $(4,5)$ . If its incentre is $(ℎ,k)$ , then $3ℎ+k$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Let the midpoints of the sides of triangle $ABC$ be $D(\frac{5}{2},7),E(\frac{5}{2},3),F(4,5)$ We have to find the incentre $(ℎ,k)$ of triangle $ABC$ . Step 1: Use the fact about the medial triangle The triangle formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of a triangle is called the medial triangle. If the midpoints are known, then the original triangle can be reconstructed using: $A=E+F-D,B=F+D-E,C=D+E-F$ Now calculate each vertex. Vertex $A$ $A=(\frac{5}{2},3)+(4,5)-(\frac{5}{2},7)$ $A=(4,1)$ Vertex $B$ $B=(4,5)+(\frac{5}{2},7)-(\frac{5}{2},3)$ $B=(4,9)$ Vertex $C$ $C=(\frac{5}{2},7)+(\frac{5}{2},3)-(4,5)$ $C=(1,5)$ So the triangle has vertices $A(4,1),B(4,9),C(1,5)$ Step 2: Find the side lengths Using distance formula: Side opposite $A$ , i.e. $BC$ $BC=\sqrt{(4-1)^{2}+(9-5)^{2}}=\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}=5$ Side opposite $B$ , i.e. $CA$ $CA=\sqrt{(4-1)^{2}+(1-5)^{2}}=\sqrt{3^{2}+(-4)^{2}}=5$ Side opposite $C$ , i.e. $AB$ $AB=\sqrt{(4-4)^{2}+(9-1)^{2}}=8$ Thus, $a=5,b=5,c=8$ Step 3: Use incentre formula The incentre of triangle with vertices $A(x_{1},y_{1})$ , $B(x_{2},y_{2})$ , $C(x_{3},y_{3})$ is $(\frac{ax_{1}+bx_{2}+cx_{3}}{a+b+c},\frac{ay_{1}+by_{2}+cy_{3}}{a+b+c})$ where $a=BC$ $b=CA$ $c=AB$ Substitute the values: $ℎ=\frac{5 \cdot 4+5 \cdot 4+8 \cdot 1}{5+5+8}=\frac{20+20+8}{18}=\frac{48}{18}=\frac{8}{3}$ $k=\frac{5 \cdot 1+5 \cdot 9+8 \cdot 5}{18}=\frac{5+45+40}{18}=\frac{90}{18}=5$ So the incentre is $(\frac{8}{3},5)$ Step 4: Find $3ℎ+k$ $3ℎ+k=3 \cdot \frac{8}{3}+5=8+5=13$ Therefore, the answer is $13$ So, the correct option is Option C .
questions.explanation_html:
Let the midpoints of the sides of triangle $ABC$ be

$D(\frac{5}{2},7),E(\frac{5}{2},3),F(4,5)$

We have to find the incentre $(ℎ,k)$ of triangle $ABC$ .

Step 1: Use the fact about the medial triangle

The triangle formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of a triangle is called the medial triangle.

If the midpoints are known, then the original triangle can be reconstructed using:

$A=E+F-D,B=F+D-E,C=D+E-F$

Now calculate each vertex.

Vertex $A$

$A=(\frac{5}{2},3)+(4,5)-(\frac{5}{2},7)$

$A=(4,1)$

Vertex $B$

$B=(4,5)+(\frac{5}{2},7)-(\frac{5}{2},3)$

$B=(4,9)$

Vertex $C$

$C=(\frac{5}{2},7)+(\frac{5}{2},3)-(4,5)$

$C=(1,5)$

So the triangle has vertices

$A(4,1),B(4,9),C(1,5)$

Step 2: Find the side lengths

Using distance formula:

Side opposite $A$ , i.e. $BC$

$BC=\sqrt{(4-1)^{2}+(9-5)^{2}}=\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}=5$

Side opposite $B$ , i.e. $CA$

$CA=\sqrt{(4-1)^{2}+(1-5)^{2}}=\sqrt{3^{2}+(-4)^{2}}=5$

Side opposite $C$ , i.e. $AB$

$AB=\sqrt{(4-4)^{2}+(9-1)^{2}}=8$

Thus,

$a=5,b=5,c=8$

Step 3: Use incentre formula

The incentre of triangle with vertices $A(x_{1},y_{1})$ , $B(x_{2},y_{2})$ , $C(x_{3},y_{3})$ is

$(\frac{ax_{1}+bx_{2}+cx_{3}}{a+b+c},\frac{ay_{1}+by_{2}+cy_{3}}{a+b+c})$

where

  • $a=BC$

  • $b=CA$

  • $c=AB$

Substitute the values:

$ℎ=\frac{5 \cdot 4+5 \cdot 4+8 \cdot 1}{5+5+8}=\frac{20+20+8}{18}=\frac{48}{18}=\frac{8}{3}$

$k=\frac{5 \cdot 1+5 \cdot 9+8 \cdot 5}{18}=\frac{5+45+40}{18}=\frac{90}{18}=5$

So the incentre is

$(\frac{8}{3},5)$

Step 4: Find $3ℎ+k$

$3ℎ+k=3 \cdot \frac{8}{3}+5=8+5=13$

Therefore, the answer is

$13$

So, the correct option is Option C.

questions.question_text: Let $A(1,2)$ and $C(-3,-6)$ be two diagonally opposite vertices of a rhombus, whose sides AD and BC are parallel to the line $7x-y=14$ . If $B(\alpha,\beta)$ and $D(\gamma,\delta)$ are the other two vertices, then $|\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta|$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $A(1,2)$ and $C(-3,-6)$ be two diagonally opposite vertices of a rhombus, whose sides AD and BC are parallel to the line $7x-y=14$ . If $B(\alpha,\beta)$ and $D(\gamma,\delta)$ are the other two vertices, then $|\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta|$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Let $A=(1,2)$ and $C=(-3,-6)$ be diagonally opposite vertices of a rhombus. In a rhombus, the diagonals bisect each other at a common point M.. Calculation of Midpoint $M$ : $\begin{aligned} & M=(\frac{1+(-3)}{2},\frac{2+(-6)}{2}) \\ & M=(\frac{-2}{2},\frac{-4}{2}) \\ & M=(-1,-2) \end{aligned}$ Since $M$ is also the midpoint of the other diagonal $BD$ where $B=(\alpha,\beta)$ and $D=(\gamma,\delta)$ : $\begin{aligned} & \frac{\alpha+\gamma}{2}=-1⟹\alpha+\gamma=-2 \\ & \frac{\beta+\delta}{2}=-2⟹\beta+\delta=-4 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & |\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta|=|(\alpha+\gamma)+(\beta+\delta)| \\ & |\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta|=|(-2)+(-4)| \\ & |\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta|=|-6| \\ & |\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta|=6 \end{aligned}$ Option (B) is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
Let $A=(1,2)$ and $C=(-3,-6)$ be diagonally opposite vertices of a rhombus.

In a rhombus, the diagonals bisect each other at a common point M..

Calculation of Midpoint $M$ :

$\begin{aligned} & M=(\frac{1+(-3)}{2},\frac{2+(-6)}{2}) \\ & M=(\frac{-2}{2},\frac{-4}{2}) \\ & M=(-1,-2) \end{aligned}$

Since $M$ is also the midpoint of the other diagonal $BD$ where $B=(\alpha,\beta)$ and $D=(\gamma,\delta)$ :

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{\alpha+\gamma}{2}=-1⟹\alpha+\gamma=-2 \\ & \frac{\beta+\delta}{2}=-2⟹\beta+\delta=-4 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & |\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta|=|(\alpha+\gamma)+(\beta+\delta)| \\ & |\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta|=|(-2)+(-4)| \\ & |\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta|=|-6| \\ & |\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta|=6 \end{aligned}$

Option (B) is correct.

questions.question_text: From the point $(-1,-1)$ , two rays are sent making angles of $45^{\circ}$ with the line $x+y=0$ . These rays get reflected from the mirror $x+2y=1$ . If the equations of the reflected rays are $ax+by=9$ and $cx+dy=7,a,b,c,d \in Z$ , then the value of $ad+bc$ is $____$ .
questions.question_html: From the point $(-1,-1)$ , two rays are sent making angles of $45^{\circ}$ with the line $x+y=0$ . These rays get reflected from the mirror $x+2y=1$ . If the equations of the reflected rays are $ax+by=9$ and $cx+dy=7,a,b,c,d \in Z$ , then the value of $ad+bc$ is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: Line $x+y=0$ has slope $-1$ . If a ray has slope $m$ and makes an angle $45^{\circ}$ with this line, then by the angle formula between two lines we use: $tan45^{\circ}=|\frac{m+1}{1-m}|$ Now $tan45^{\circ}=1$ , so we get: $\rightarrow \pm 1=\frac{m+1}{1-m}$ Solving this gives two possible directions. One solution gives a horizontal line ( $m=0$ ), and the other corresponds to a vertical line (perpendicular to the $x$ -axis). $\rightarrow m=0$ & one line is perpendicular to x axis. Both rays start from $(-1,-1)$ , so the two incident rays are: $L_{1}$ : $x=-1$ , $L_{2}$ : $y=-1$ Next, each ray reflects from the mirror line $x+2y=1$ . To get the reflected ray, we take the mirror image of the incident line in the mirror. First, take the mirror image of $x+1=0$ in $x+2y=1$ . Now taking mirror image of $x+1=0$ in $x+2y=1$ $A^{'}:\frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{-2(-1-2-1)}{1^{2}+2^{2}}$ From this, we get the image point: $x=\frac{3}{5},y=\frac{11}{5}A^{'}(\frac{3}{5},\frac{11}{5})$ So the corresponding reflected line is written as: line $=3x-4y+7=0$ Similarly, take the mirror image of $y+1=0$ in $x+2y=1$ . Now taking mirror image of $y+1=0$ in $x+2y=1$ $A^{''}:\frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{-2(-1-2-1)}{1^{2}+2^{2}}$ This again gives: $x=\frac{3}{5},y=\frac{11}{5}$ $A^{''}(\frac{3}{5},\frac{11}{5})$ Now write the equation of the reflected line using point-slope form: line : $(y+1)=\frac{(\frac{11}{5}+1)}{(\frac{3}{5}-3)}(x-3)$ Simplifying gives one reflected ray as: $4x+3y=9$ Compare $4x+3y=9$ with $ax+by=9$ . Then: comparing $4x+3y=9$ with $ax+by=9$ & $a=4$ , $b=3$ The other reflected ray is written as: by line $-3x+4y=7$ Compare $-3x+4y=7$ with $cx+dy=7$ . Then: comparing with $cx+dy=7$ $\therefore c=-3$ , $d=4$ Now calculate $ad+bc$ : So, $ad+bc$ $=4 \times 4+3 \times (-3)$ $=16-9=7$

Now $tan45^{\circ}=1$ , so we get:

Solving this gives two possible directions. One solution gives a horizontal line ( $m=0$ ), and the other corresponds to a vertical line (perpendicular to the $x$ -axis).

$\rightarrow m=0$ & one line is perpendicular to x axis.

Both rays start from $(-1,-1)$ , so the two incident rays are:

Next, each ray reflects from the mirror line $x+2y=1$ . To get the reflected ray, we take the mirror image of the incident line in the mirror.

Now taking mirror image of $x+1=0$ in $x+2y=1$

$A^{'}:\frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{-2(-1-2-1)}{1^{2}+2^{2}}$

From this, we get the image point:

$x=\frac{3}{5},y=\frac{11}{5}A^{'}(\frac{3}{5},\frac{11}{5})$

So the corresponding reflected line is written as:

line $=3x-4y+7=0$

$A^{''}(\frac{3}{5},\frac{11}{5})$

Now write the equation of the reflected line using point-slope form:

line :

Simplifying gives one reflected ray as:

comparing $4x+3y=9$ with $ax+by=9$ &

$a=4$ , $b=3$

The other reflected ray is written as:

by line

$-3x+4y=7$

Compare $-3x+4y=7$ with $cx+dy=7$ . Then:

comparing with

$cx+dy=7$

$\therefore c=-3$ , $d=4$

Now calculate $ad+bc$ :

So, $ad+bc$

$=4 \times 4+3 \times (-3)$

$=16-9=7$

questions.question_text: In an equilateral triangle $PQR$ , let the vertex $P$ be at $(3,5)$ and the side $QR$ be along the line $x+y=4$ . If the orthocentre of the triangle PQR is $(\alpha,\beta)$ , then $9(\alpha+\beta)$ is equal to:
questions.question_html: In an equilateral triangle $PQR$ , let the vertex $P$ be at $(3,5)$ and the side $QR$ be along the line $x+y=4$ . If the orthocentre of the triangle PQR is $(\alpha,\beta)$ , then $9(\alpha+\beta)$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Since $QR$ lies on the line $x+y=4,$ and $P=(3,5)$ , first find the altitude from $P$ to the side $QR$ . In an equilateral triangle, all altitudes, medians and angle bisectors coincide. Also, the orthocentre lies on the altitude from each vertex and divides the altitude in the ratio $2:1$ from the vertex. So let us proceed step by step. The line $QR$ has equation $x+y-4=0.$ Distance of point $P(3,5)$ from this line is $d=\frac{|3+5-4|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}=2\sqrt{2}.$ This is the altitude of the equilateral triangle from vertex $P$ . Now, the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line $x+y=4$ lies on the altitude. Since in an equilateral triangle the orthocentre lies at $\frac{2}{3}$ of the altitude from the vertex, we can find it along the perpendicular direction. The slope of $x+y=4$ is $-1$ , so the perpendicular slope is $1$ . Hence the altitude through $P(3,5)$ is $y-5=1(x-3)$ or $y=x+2.$ The orthocentre lies on this line. Now find the foot of perpendicular from $P$ to $x+y=4$ by solving $y=x+2$ and $x+y=4.$ Substitute $y=x+2$ into $x+y=4$ : $x+(x+2)=4$ $2x=2$ $x=1,y=3.$ So the foot is $(1,3)$ . Thus the altitude segment is from $P(3,5)$ to $(1,3)$ . The orthocentre divides this altitude in the ratio $2:1$ from vertex $P$ . Therefore, $H=(\frac{2 \cdot 1+1 \cdot 3}{3},\frac{2 \cdot 3+1 \cdot 5}{3})$ This is incorrect ratio placement, so let us use the correct section carefully: If $H$ divides the segment from $P$ to foot $D$ in the ratio $2:1$ , then $H=P+\frac{2}{3}(D-P).$ Here, $D-P=(1-3,3-5)=(-2,-2).$ So $H=(3,5)+\frac{2}{3}(-2,-2)=(3-\frac{4}{3},5-\frac{4}{3})=(\frac{5}{3},\frac{11}{3}).$ Thus, $\alpha=\frac{5}{3},\beta=\frac{11}{3}.$ So, $\alpha+\beta=\frac{5}{3}+\frac{11}{3}=\frac{16}{3}.$ Therefore, $9(\alpha+\beta)=9 \cdot \frac{16}{3}=48.$ Hence the correct answer is $48$ So, Option D is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
Since $QR$ lies on the line

$x+y=4,$

and $P=(3,5)$ , first find the altitude from $P$ to the side $QR$ .

In an equilateral triangle, all altitudes, medians and angle bisectors coincide. Also, the orthocentre lies on the altitude from each vertex and divides the altitude in the ratio $2:1$ from the vertex.

So let us proceed step by step.

The line $QR$ has equation

$x+y-4=0.$

Distance of point $P(3,5)$ from this line is

$d=\frac{|3+5-4|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}=2\sqrt{2}.$

This is the altitude of the equilateral triangle from vertex $P$ .

Now, the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line $x+y=4$ lies on the altitude. Since in an equilateral triangle the orthocentre lies at $\frac{2}{3}$ of the altitude from the vertex, we can find it along the perpendicular direction.

The slope of $x+y=4$ is $-1$ , so the perpendicular slope is $1$ .

Hence the altitude through $P(3,5)$ is

$y-5=1(x-3)$

or

$y=x+2.$

The orthocentre lies on this line.

Now find the foot of perpendicular from $P$ to $x+y=4$ by solving

$y=x+2$

and

$x+y=4.$

Substitute $y=x+2$ into $x+y=4$ :

$x+(x+2)=4$

$2x=2$

$x=1,y=3.$

So the foot is $(1,3)$ .

Thus the altitude segment is from $P(3,5)$ to $(1,3)$ .

The orthocentre divides this altitude in the ratio $2:1$ from vertex $P$ . Therefore,

$H=(\frac{2 \cdot 1+1 \cdot 3}{3},\frac{2 \cdot 3+1 \cdot 5}{3})$

This is incorrect ratio placement, so let us use the correct section carefully:

If $H$ divides the segment from $P$ to foot $D$ in the ratio $2:1$ , then

$H=P+\frac{2}{3}(D-P).$

Here,

$D-P=(1-3,3-5)=(-2,-2).$

So

$H=(3,5)+\frac{2}{3}(-2,-2)=(3-\frac{4}{3},5-\frac{4}{3})=(\frac{5}{3},\frac{11}{3}).$

Thus,

$\alpha=\frac{5}{3},\beta=\frac{11}{3}.$

So,

$\alpha+\beta=\frac{5}{3}+\frac{11}{3}=\frac{16}{3}.$

Therefore,

$9(\alpha+\beta)=9 \cdot \frac{16}{3}=48.$

Hence the correct answer is

$48$

So, Option D is correct.

questions.question_text: Let ABC be an equilateral triangle with orthocenter at the origin and the side BC on the line $x+2\sqrt{2}y=4$ . If the co-ordinates of the vertex A are $(\alpha,\beta)$ , then the greatest integer less than or equal to $|\alpha+\sqrt{2}\beta|$ is
questions.question_html: Let ABC be an equilateral triangle with orthocenter at the origin and the side BC on the line $x+2\sqrt{2}y=4$ . If the co-ordinates of the vertex A are $(\alpha,\beta)$ , then the greatest integer less than or equal to $|\alpha+\sqrt{2}\beta|$ is
questions.explanation_text: $\text{Orthocenter}(O):(0,0)\text{. Since it’s an equilateral triangle, this is also the Centroid.}$ Side BC Line : $x+2\sqrt{2}y=4$ . Vertex A : $(\alpha,\beta)$ . Find the distance from the Centroid to side BC The side $BC$ lies on the line $x+2\sqrt{2}y-4=0$ . The distance from the origin $G(0,0)$ to this line is the length of the "lower" part of the median ( $r$ ). Using the point-to-line distance formula : $r=\frac{|0+2\sqrt{2}(0)-4|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}}=\frac{|-4|}{\sqrt{1+8}}=\frac{4}{3}$ Find the coordinates of Vertex $A(\alpha,\beta)$ The centroid $G$ divides the segment $AD$ (where $D$ is the foot of the altitude on $BC$ ) in the ratio $2:1$ . Therefore, the distance from $A$ to $G$ is $2r$ . $AG=2 \times \frac{4}{3}=\frac{8}{3}$ The line $AG$ is perpendicular to side $BC$ . The slope of $BC$ is $m=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ , so the slope of the line $AG$ (the altitude) is the negative reciprocal: $m_{⟂}=2\sqrt{2}$ Since $A$ lies on the line passing through the origin with slope $2\sqrt{2}$ , its coordinates can be written as: $\alpha=k,\beta=2\sqrt{2}k$ Because $A$ and the side $BC$ are on opposite sides of the origin (the centroid), and the constant term in our line equation is negative, $A$ must satisfy the condition that its position yields an opposite sign. Substituting these into the distance formula $AG=\frac{8}{3}$ : $\sqrt{k^{2}+(2\sqrt{2}k)^{2}}=\frac{8}{3}⟹\sqrt{9k^{2}}=\frac{8}{3}⟹3|k|=\frac{8}{3}⟹|k|=\frac{8}{9}$ Calculate $|\alpha+\sqrt{2}\beta|$ Substitute $\alpha=k$ and $\beta=2\sqrt{2}k$ : $|\alpha+\sqrt{2}\beta|=|k+\sqrt{2}(2\sqrt{2}k)|$ $=|k+4k|=|5k|$ $=5 \times \frac{8}{9}=\frac{40}{9} \approx 4.44$ greatest integer less than or equal to $|\alpha+\sqrt{2}\beta|=[4.44]=4$ .

  1. Find the distance from the Centroid to side BC

The side $BC$ lies on the line $x+2\sqrt{2}y-4=0$ . The distance from the origin $G(0,0)$ to this line is the length of the "lower" part of the median ( $r$ ).

$\alpha=k,\beta=2\sqrt{2}k$

Because $A$ and the side $BC$ are on opposite sides of the origin (the centroid), and the constant term in our line equation is negative, $A$ must satisfy the condition that its position yields an opposite sign. Substituting these into the distance formula $AG=\frac{8}{3}$ :

  1. Calculate $|\alpha+\sqrt{2}\beta|$

Substitute $\alpha=k$ and $\beta=2\sqrt{2}k$ :

$|\alpha+\sqrt{2}\beta|=|k+\sqrt{2}(2\sqrt{2}k)|$

$=|k+4k|=|5k|$

$=5 \times \frac{8}{9}=\frac{40}{9} \approx 4.44$

The line segment $AB$ meets the angle bisector of the given half-lines at the point $Q$ . If $PQ=\frac{9}{2}$ and $R$ is the radius of the circumcircle of $△PAB$ , then $\frac{\alpha^{2}}{R}$ is equal to $____$

questions.explanation_text: The two half-lines are given by $x-\sqrt{3}|y|=\alpha,\alpha>0$ We will first understand their geometry. 1. Find the two half-lines and their point of intersection Since $|y|$ is present, we split into two cases: Case 1: $y \ge 0$ $x-\sqrt{3}y=\alpha$ Case 2: $y \le 0$ $x+\sqrt{3}y=\alpha$ These are two lines meeting at the point $P$ . To find their intersection, put $y=0$ in either equation: $x=\alpha$ So, $P=(\alpha,0)$ Thus the two half-lines start from $P$ and go outward along these two lines. 2. Find points $A$ and $B$ Points $A$ and $B$ lie on these two half-lines and are each at distance $\alpha$ from $P$ . Let $A$ be on the upper line $x-\sqrt{3}y=\alpha$ and $B$ on the lower line $x+\sqrt{3}y=\alpha$ . The slope of the upper line is $y=\frac{x-\alpha}{\sqrt{3}} \Rightarrow m=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ So this line makes angle $30^{\circ}$ with the positive $x$ -axis. Similarly, the lower line makes angle $-30^{\circ}$ with the positive $x$ -axis. Hence the angle between the two half-lines is $60^{\circ}$ Since $PA=\alpha$ and $PB=\alpha$ , the points are obtained by moving distance $\alpha$ from $P=(\alpha,0)$ along directions $\pm 30^{\circ}$ . Therefore, $A=(\alpha+\alpha cos30^{\circ},\alpha sin30^{\circ})$ $B=(\alpha+\alpha cos30^{\circ},-\alpha sin30^{\circ})$ Using $cos30^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $sin30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$ , $A=(\alpha+\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2},\frac{\alpha}{2})$ $B=(\alpha+\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2},-\frac{\alpha}{2})$ 3. Find the angle bisector and point $Q$ The figure is symmetric about the $x$ -axis, so the angle bisector of the two half-lines is the positive $x$ -axis. Also, $A$ and $B$ have the same $x$ -coordinate, so $AB$ is a vertical segment. Hence $AB$ meets the $x$ -axis at $Q=(\alpha+\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2},0)$ So, $PQ=(\alpha+\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2})-\alpha=\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2}$ Given that $PQ=\frac{9}{2}$ therefore, $\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2}=\frac{9}{2}$ So, $\sqrt{3}\alpha=9$ $\alpha=\frac{9}{\sqrt{3}}=3\sqrt{3}$ Hence, $\alpha^{2}=(3\sqrt{3})^{2}=27$ 4. Find circumradius $R$ of $△PAB$ In $△PAB$ , $PA=PB=\alpha$ and the included angle $\angleAPB=60^{\circ}$ So the triangle is actually equilateral, because $AB^{2}=\alpha^{2}+\alpha^{2}-2\alpha^{2}cos60^{\circ}=2\alpha^{2}-\alpha^{2}=\alpha^{2}$ Thus, $AB=\alpha$ Hence $△PAB$ is equilateral with side $\alpha$ . For an equilateral triangle of side $a$ , circumradius is $R=\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}$ So here, $R=\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{3}}$ Using $\alpha=3\sqrt{3}$ , $R=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}=3$ 5. Compute $\frac{\alpha^{2}}{R}$ $\frac{\alpha^{2}}{R}=\frac{27}{3}=9$ Therefore, the required value is $9$
questions.explanation_html:
The two half-lines are given by

$x-\sqrt{3}|y|=\alpha,\alpha>0$

We will first understand their geometry.

1. Find the two half-lines and their point of intersection

Since $|y|$ is present, we split into two cases:

Case 1: $y \ge 0$

$x-\sqrt{3}y=\alpha$

Case 2: $y \le 0$

$x+\sqrt{3}y=\alpha$

These are two lines meeting at the point $P$ .

To find their intersection, put $y=0$ in either equation:

$x=\alpha$

So,

$P=(\alpha,0)$

Thus the two half-lines start from $P$ and go outward along these two lines.

2. Find points $A$ and $B$

Points $A$ and $B$ lie on these two half-lines and are each at distance $\alpha$ from $P$ .

Let $A$ be on the upper line $x-\sqrt{3}y=\alpha$ and $B$ on the lower line $x+\sqrt{3}y=\alpha$ .

The slope of the upper line is

$y=\frac{x-\alpha}{\sqrt{3}} \Rightarrow m=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

So this line makes angle $30^{\circ}$ with the positive $x$ -axis.

Similarly, the lower line makes angle $-30^{\circ}$ with the positive $x$ -axis.

Hence the angle between the two half-lines is

$60^{\circ}$

Since $PA=\alpha$ and $PB=\alpha$ , the points are obtained by moving distance $\alpha$ from $P=(\alpha,0)$ along directions $\pm 30^{\circ}$ .

Therefore,

$A=(\alpha+\alpha cos30^{\circ},\alpha sin30^{\circ})$

$B=(\alpha+\alpha cos30^{\circ},-\alpha sin30^{\circ})$

Using $cos30^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $sin30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$ ,

$A=(\alpha+\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2},\frac{\alpha}{2})$

$B=(\alpha+\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2},-\frac{\alpha}{2})$

3. Find the angle bisector and point $Q$

The figure is symmetric about the $x$ -axis, so the angle bisector of the two half-lines is the positive $x$ -axis.

Also, $A$ and $B$ have the same $x$ -coordinate, so $AB$ is a vertical segment.

Hence $AB$ meets the $x$ -axis at

$Q=(\alpha+\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2},0)$

So,

$PQ=(\alpha+\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2})-\alpha=\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2}$

Given that

$PQ=\frac{9}{2}$

therefore,

$\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha}{2}=\frac{9}{2}$

So,

$\sqrt{3}\alpha=9$

$\alpha=\frac{9}{\sqrt{3}}=3\sqrt{3}$

Hence,

$\alpha^{2}=(3\sqrt{3})^{2}=27$

4. Find circumradius $R$ of $△PAB$

In $△PAB$ ,

$PA=PB=\alpha$

and the included angle

$\angleAPB=60^{\circ}$

So the triangle is actually equilateral, because

$AB^{2}=\alpha^{2}+\alpha^{2}-2\alpha^{2}cos60^{\circ}=2\alpha^{2}-\alpha^{2}=\alpha^{2}$

Thus,

$AB=\alpha$

Hence $△PAB$ is equilateral with side $\alpha$ .

For an equilateral triangle of side $a$ , circumradius is

$R=\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}$

So here,

$R=\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{3}}$

Using $\alpha=3\sqrt{3}$ ,

$R=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}=3$

5. Compute $\frac{\alpha^{2}}{R}$

$\frac{\alpha^{2}}{R}=\frac{27}{3}=9$

Therefore, the required value is

$9$

questions.question_text: Let the line $L_{1}:x+3=0$ intersect the lines $L_{2}:x-y=0$ and $L_{3}:3x+y=0$ at the points A and B , respectively. Let the bisector of the obtuse angle between the lines $L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$ intersect the line $L_{1}$ at the point $C$ . Then $BC^{2}:AC^{2}$ is equal to:
questions.question_html: Let the line $L_{1}:x+3=0$ intersect the lines $L_{2}:x-y=0$ and $L_{3}:3x+y=0$ at the points A and B , respectively. Let the bisector of the obtuse angle between the lines $L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$ intersect the line $L_{1}$ at the point $C$ . Then $BC^{2}:AC^{2}$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Given: $L_{1}:x+3=0 \Rightarrow x=-3$ $L_{2}:x-y=0 \Rightarrow y=x$ $L_{3}:3x+y=0 \Rightarrow y=-3x$ We first find points $A$ and $B$ . 1. Coordinates of $A$ Point $A$ is the intersection of $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ . Since $x=-3$ and $y=x$ , we get $y=-3$ So, $A=(-3,-3)$ 2. Coordinates of $B$ Point $B$ is the intersection of $L_{1}$ and $L_{3}$ . Since $x=-3$ and $y=-3x$ , we get $y=-3(-3)=9$ So, $B=(-3,9)$ 3. Equation of angle bisectors of $L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$ The lines are: $L_{2}:x-y=0$ $L_{3}:3x+y=0$ Angle bisectors are given by $\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}= \pm \frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{3^{2}+1^{2}}}$ That is, $\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{2}}= \pm \frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{10}}$ We need the bisector of the obtuse angle. Let us find its slope. Since both lines pass through the origin, we can use the formula for slope of angle bisectors. The slopes of $L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$ are: for $L_{2}$ , $m_{1}=1$ for $L_{3}$ , $m_{2}=-3$ The acute angle bisector lies between the directions of these lines, and the obtuse angle bisector is the other one. Now let us find the bisector which intersects $x=-3$ between $y=-3$ and $y=9$ or outside, by solving directly. Substitute $x=-3$ into angle bisector equations. 4. Find point $C$ From $\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{10}}$ put $x=-3$ : $\frac{-3-y}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{-9+y}{\sqrt{10}}$ Cross-multiplying: $\sqrt{10}(-3-y)=\sqrt{2}(-9+y)$ This gives one point on $L_{1}$ . From $\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{2}}=-\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{10}}$ put $x=-3$ : $\frac{-3-y}{\sqrt{2}}=-\frac{-9+y}{\sqrt{10}}$ Instead of solving both, it is easier to use the fact that any point on the angle bisector is equidistant from the two lines. Let $C=(-3,k)$ on $L_{1}$ . Distance of $C$ from $L_{2}:x-y=0$ is $\frac{|x-y|}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{|-3-k|}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{|k+3|}{\sqrt{2}}$ Distance of $C$ from $L_{3}:3x+y=0$ is $\frac{|3x+y|}{\sqrt{10}}=\frac{|-9+k|}{\sqrt{10}}=\frac{|k-9|}{\sqrt{10}}$ So, $\frac{|k+3|}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{|k-9|}{\sqrt{10}}$ Squaring: $\frac{(k+3)^{2}}{2}=\frac{(k-9)^{2}}{10}$ $5(k+3)^{2}=(k-9)^{2}$ Expand: $5(k^{2}+6k+9)=k^{2}-18k+81$ $5k^{2}+30k+45=k^{2}-18k+81$ $4k^{2}+48k-36=0$ $k^{2}+12k-9=0$ $k=-6 \pm 3\sqrt{5}$ So the two bisectors meet $L_{1}$ at points with $y=-6+3\sqrt{5}$ and $y=-6-3\sqrt{5}$ . Now $A=(-3,-3)$ and $B=(-3,9)$ . The obtuse angle is the larger angle between $L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$ . Its bisector lies inside that larger region, which is the bisector with slope closer to negative small value, and it cuts $x=-3$ at the point between $A$ and $B$ . Since $-6+3\sqrt{5} \approx 0.708$ this lies between $-3$ and $9$ . Hence, $C=(-3,-6+3\sqrt{5})$ 5. Find $AC^{2}$ and $BC^{2}$ Since all three points have the same $x$ -coordinate, distances depend only on $y$ -coordinates. $AC$ $AC=|-6+3\sqrt{5}-(-3)|=|-3+3\sqrt{5}|=3(\sqrt{5}-1)$ So, $AC^{2}=9(\sqrt{5}-1)^{2}$ $BC$ $BC=|9-(-6+3\sqrt{5})|=|15-3\sqrt{5}|=3(5-\sqrt{5})$ So, $BC^{2}=9(5-\sqrt{5})^{2}$ Therefore, $BC^{2}:AC^{2}=(5-\sqrt{5})^{2}:(\sqrt{5}-1)^{2}$ Now, $(5-\sqrt{5})^{2}=25+5-10\sqrt{5}=30-10\sqrt{5}=10(3-\sqrt{5})$ and $(\sqrt{5}-1)^{2}=5+1-2\sqrt{5}=6-2\sqrt{5}=2(3-\sqrt{5})$ Hence, $BC^{2}:AC^{2}=10(3-\sqrt{5}):2(3-\sqrt{5})=5:1$ So the required ratio is $5:1$ Hence, the correct option is $\text{A}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given:

  • $L_{1}:x+3=0 \Rightarrow x=-3$

  • $L_{2}:x-y=0 \Rightarrow y=x$

  • $L_{3}:3x+y=0 \Rightarrow y=-3x$

We first find points $A$ and $B$ .

1. Coordinates of $A$

Point $A$ is the intersection of $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ .

Since $x=-3$ and $y=x$ , we get

$y=-3$

So,

$A=(-3,-3)$

2. Coordinates of $B$

Point $B$ is the intersection of $L_{1}$ and $L_{3}$ .

Since $x=-3$ and $y=-3x$ , we get

$y=-3(-3)=9$

So,

$B=(-3,9)$

3. Equation of angle bisectors of $L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$

The lines are:

$L_{2}:x-y=0$

$L_{3}:3x+y=0$

Angle bisectors are given by

$\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}= \pm \frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{3^{2}+1^{2}}}$

That is,

$\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{2}}= \pm \frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{10}}$

We need the bisector of the obtuse angle.

Let us find its slope.

Since both lines pass through the origin, we can use the formula for slope of angle bisectors.

The slopes of $L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$ are:

  • for $L_{2}$ , $m_{1}=1$

  • for $L_{3}$ , $m_{2}=-3$

The acute angle bisector lies between the directions of these lines, and the obtuse angle bisector is the other one.

Now let us find the bisector which intersects $x=-3$ between $y=-3$ and $y=9$ or outside, by solving directly.

Substitute $x=-3$ into angle bisector equations.

4. Find point $C$

From

$\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{10}}$

put $x=-3$ :

$\frac{-3-y}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{-9+y}{\sqrt{10}}$

Cross-multiplying:

$\sqrt{10}(-3-y)=\sqrt{2}(-9+y)$

This gives one point on $L_{1}$ .

From

$\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{2}}=-\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{10}}$

put $x=-3$ :

$\frac{-3-y}{\sqrt{2}}=-\frac{-9+y}{\sqrt{10}}$

Instead of solving both, it is easier to use the fact that any point on the angle bisector is equidistant from the two lines.

Let $C=(-3,k)$ on $L_{1}$ .

Distance of $C$ from $L_{2}:x-y=0$ is

$\frac{|x-y|}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{|-3-k|}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{|k+3|}{\sqrt{2}}$

Distance of $C$ from $L_{3}:3x+y=0$ is

$\frac{|3x+y|}{\sqrt{10}}=\frac{|-9+k|}{\sqrt{10}}=\frac{|k-9|}{\sqrt{10}}$

So,

$\frac{|k+3|}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{|k-9|}{\sqrt{10}}$

Squaring:

$\frac{(k+3)^{2}}{2}=\frac{(k-9)^{2}}{10}$

$5(k+3)^{2}=(k-9)^{2}$

Expand:

$5(k^{2}+6k+9)=k^{2}-18k+81$

$5k^{2}+30k+45=k^{2}-18k+81$

$4k^{2}+48k-36=0$

$k^{2}+12k-9=0$

$k=-6 \pm 3\sqrt{5}$

So the two bisectors meet $L_{1}$ at points with $y=-6+3\sqrt{5}$ and $y=-6-3\sqrt{5}$ .

Now $A=(-3,-3)$ and $B=(-3,9)$ .

The obtuse angle is the larger angle between $L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$ .

Its bisector lies inside that larger region, which is the bisector with slope closer to negative small value, and it cuts $x=-3$ at the point between $A$ and $B$ .

Since

$-6+3\sqrt{5} \approx 0.708$

this lies between $-3$ and $9$ .

Hence,

$C=(-3,-6+3\sqrt{5})$

5. Find $AC^{2}$ and $BC^{2}$

Since all three points have the same $x$ -coordinate, distances depend only on $y$ -coordinates.

$AC$

$AC=|-6+3\sqrt{5}-(-3)|=|-3+3\sqrt{5}|=3(\sqrt{5}-1)$

So,

$AC^{2}=9(\sqrt{5}-1)^{2}$

$BC$

$BC=|9-(-6+3\sqrt{5})|=|15-3\sqrt{5}|=3(5-\sqrt{5})$

So,

$BC^{2}=9(5-\sqrt{5})^{2}$

Therefore,

$BC^{2}:AC^{2}=(5-\sqrt{5})^{2}:(\sqrt{5}-1)^{2}$

Now,

$(5-\sqrt{5})^{2}=25+5-10\sqrt{5}=30-10\sqrt{5}=10(3-\sqrt{5})$

and

$(\sqrt{5}-1)^{2}=5+1-2\sqrt{5}=6-2\sqrt{5}=2(3-\sqrt{5})$

Hence,

$BC^{2}:AC^{2}=10(3-\sqrt{5}):2(3-\sqrt{5})=5:1$

So the required ratio is

$5:1$

Hence, the correct option is $\text{A}$ .

questions.question_html: Let the angles made with the positive $x$ -axis by two straight lines drawn from the point $P(2,3)$ and meeting the line $x+y=6$ at a distance $\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$ from the point P be $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ . Then the value of $(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2})$ is:
questions.explanation_text: Let any point $Q(t,6-t)$ on line $x+y=6$ such that. distance $PQ=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \Rightarrow PQ^{2}=\frac{2}{3}$ . using distance formula for points $P(2,3)$ and $Q(t,6-t)$ . $\begin{aligned} & (2-t)^{2}+(3-6+t)^{2}=\frac{2}{3} \\ & (2-t)^{2}+(t-3)^{2}=\frac{2}{3} \\ & 4+t^{2}-4t+t^{2}+9-6t=\frac{2}{3} \\ & 2t^{2}-10t+13=\frac{2}{3} \\ & 6t^{2}-30t+39-2=0 \\ & 6t^{2}-30t+37=0 \end{aligned}$ let $t_{1}&t_{2}$ are roots of this equation. $t_{1}+t_{2}=\frac{30}{6}=5\text{and}t_{1}t_{2}=\frac{37}{6}.$ So, there are two point $Q_{1}(t_{1},6-t_{1})&Q_{2}(t_{2},6-t_{2})$ . It is given that angle made with positive x -axis by straight lines from $P(2,3)$ to $Q_{1}&Q_{2}$ is $\theta_{1}&\theta_{2}$ respectively. This means $tan\theta_{1}=$ slope of line $PQ_{1}$ . $tan\theta_{1}=\frac{3-(6-t_{1})}{2-t_{1}} \Rightarrow \theta_{1}=\frac{t_{1}-3}{2-t_{1}}$ similarly, $tan\theta_{2}=$ slope of line $PQ_{2}$ $tan\theta_{2}=\frac{t_{2}-3}{2-t_{2}} \Rightarrow \theta_{2}=tan^{-1}(\frac{t_{2}-3}{2-t_{2}})$ adding equation (1) \& (2) $\begin{aligned} & \theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=tan^{-1}(\frac{t_{1}-3}{2-t_{1}})+tan^{-1}(\frac{t_{2}-3}{2-t_{2}}) \\ & =tan^{-1}⎛⎝⎜\frac{\frac{t_{1}-3}{2-t_{1}}+\frac{t_{2}-3}{2-t_{2}}}{1-(\frac{t_{1}-3}{2-t_{1}})(\frac{t_{2}-3}{2-t_{2}})}⎞⎠⎟,\text{use}tan^{-1}x+tan^{-1}y=tan^{-1}(\frac{x+y}{1-xy}) \\ & =tan^{-1}\frac{2t_{1}-6-t_{1}t_{2}+3t_{1}+2t_{2}-6-t_{1}t_{2}+3t_{1}}{4-2(t_{1}+t_{2})+t_{1}t_{2}-(9-3(t_{1}+t_{2})+t_{1}t_{2})} \\ & \theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=tan^{-1}\frac{5(t_{1}+t_{2})-2t_{1}t_{2}-12}{(t_{1}+t_{2})-5} \end{aligned}$ substitute value of $t_{1}+t_{2}=5&t_{1}t_{2}=\frac{37}{6}$ $\begin{aligned} & \theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=tan^{-1}\frac{5 \times 5-2 \times \frac{37}{6}-12}{5-5} \\ & \theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=tan^{-1}(\infty)=\frac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$

let $t_{1}&t_{2}$ are roots of this equation.

So, there are two point $Q_{1}(t_{1},6-t_{1})&Q_{2}(t_{2},6-t_{2})$ .

It is given that angle made with positive x -axis by straight lines from $P(2,3)$ to $Q_{1}&Q_{2}$ is $\theta_{1}&\theta_{2}$ respectively.

This means $tan\theta_{1}=$ slope of line $PQ_{1}$ .

$tan\theta_{1}=\frac{3-(6-t_{1})}{2-t_{1}} \Rightarrow \theta_{1}=\frac{t_{1}-3}{2-t_{1}}$

similarly, $tan\theta_{2}=$ slope of line $PQ_{2}$

$tan\theta_{2}=\frac{t_{2}-3}{2-t_{2}} \Rightarrow \theta_{2}=tan^{-1}(\frac{t_{2}-3}{2-t_{2}})$

adding equation (1) \& (2)

$\begin{aligned} & \theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=tan^{-1}(\frac{t_{1}-3}{2-t_{1}})+tan^{-1}(\frac{t_{2}-3}{2-t_{2}}) \\ & =tan^{-1}⎛⎝⎜\frac{\frac{t_{1}-3}{2-t_{1}}+\frac{t_{2}-3}{2-t_{2}}}{1-(\frac{t_{1}-3}{2-t_{1}})(\frac{t_{2}-3}{2-t_{2}})}⎞⎠⎟,\text{use}tan^{-1}x+tan^{-1}y=tan^{-1}(\frac{x+y}{1-xy}) \\ & =tan^{-1}\frac{2t_{1}-6-t_{1}t_{2}+3t_{1}+2t_{2}-6-t_{1}t_{2}+3t_{1}}{4-2(t_{1}+t_{2})+t_{1}t_{2}-(9-3(t_{1}+t_{2})+t_{1}t_{2})} \\ & \theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=tan^{-1}\frac{5(t_{1}+t_{2})-2t_{1}t_{2}-12}{(t_{1}+t_{2})-5} \end{aligned}$

substitute value of $t_{1}+t_{2}=5&t_{1}t_{2}=\frac{37}{6}$

$\begin{aligned} & \theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=tan^{-1}\frac{5 \times 5-2 \times \frac{37}{6}-12}{5-5} \\ & \theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=tan^{-1}(\infty)=\frac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let the vertex A of a triangle ABC be $(1,2)$ , and the mid-point of the side AB be $(5,-1)$ . If the centroid of this triangle is $(3,4)$ and its circumcenter is $(\alpha,\beta)$ , then $21(\alpha+\beta)$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let the vertex A of a triangle ABC be $(1,2)$ , and the mid-point of the side AB be $(5,-1)$ . If the centroid of this triangle is $(3,4)$ and its circumcenter is $(\alpha,\beta)$ , then $21(\alpha+\beta)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Let the coordinates of vertex B be $(x_{B},y_{B})$ . We are given that vertex A is $(1,2)$ and the mid-point of side AB is $(5,-1)$ . Using the mid-point formula, the coordinates of the mid-point are given by: $(\frac{x_{A}+x_{B}}{2},\frac{y_{A}+y_{B}}{2})=(5,-1)$ By equating the $x$ and $y$ coordinates, we get: $\frac{1+x_{B}}{2}=5⟹1+x_{B}=10⟹x_{B}=9$ $\frac{2+y_{B}}{2}=-1⟹2+y_{B}=-2⟹y_{B}=-4$ So, the coordinates of vertex B are $(9,-4)$ . Let the coordinates of vertex C be $(x_{C},y_{C})$ . The centroid of a triangle with vertices $(x_{1},y_{1})$ , $(x_{2},y_{2})$ , and $(x_{3},y_{3})$ is given by the formula: $(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}}{3},\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}}{3})$ We are given the centroid of triangle ABC is $(3,4)$ . Using the coordinates of vertices A, B, and C: $\frac{1+9+x_{C}}{3}=3⟹10+x_{C}=9⟹x_{C}=-1$ $\frac{2+(-4)+y_{C}}{3}=4⟹-2+y_{C}=12⟹y_{C}=14$ So, the coordinates of vertex C are $(-1,14)$ . The circumcenter of a triangle is a point that is equidistant from all three of its vertices. Let the given circumcenter be marked as $O(\alpha,\beta)$ . Therefore, we have: $OA=OB=OC⟹OA^{2}=OB^{2}=OC^{2}$ Using the distance formula, we will write the equations for the squares of the distances: $OA^{2}=(\alpha-1)^{2}+(\beta-2)^{2}=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-2\alpha-4\beta+5$ $OB^{2}=(\alpha-9)^{2}+(\beta+4)^{2}=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-18\alpha+8\beta+97$ $OC^{2}=(\alpha+1)^{2}+(\beta-14)^{2}=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+2\alpha-28\beta+197$ Now, equating $OA^{2}=OB^{2}$ : $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-2\alpha-4\beta+5=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-18\alpha+8\beta+97$ $16\alpha-12\beta=92$ Dividing the entire equation by 4 gives our first linear equation: $4\alpha-3\beta=23\text{--- (Equation 1)}$ Next, equating $OA^{2}=OC^{2}$ : $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-2\alpha-4\beta+5=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+2\alpha-28\beta+197$ $-4\alpha+24\beta=192$ Dividing this equation by -4 gives our second linear equation: $\alpha-6\beta=-48⟹\alpha=6\beta-48\text{--- (Equation 2)}$ Substitute the expression for $\alpha$ from Equation 2 into Equation 1: $4(6\beta-48)-3\beta=23$ $24\beta-192-3\beta=23$ $21\beta-192=23$ $21\beta=215⟹\beta=\frac{215}{21}$ Now, substitute the value of $\beta$ back into Equation 2 to find $\alpha$ : $\alpha=6(\frac{215}{21})-48$ $\alpha=\frac{1290}{21}-\frac{1008}{21}$ $\alpha=\frac{282}{21}$ The problem asks for the value of $21(\alpha+\beta)$ . We can simply plug in our values: $21(\alpha+\beta)=21(\frac{282}{21}+\frac{215}{21})$ $21(\alpha+\beta)=282+215=497$ Option C is the correct answer.
questions.explanation_html:
Let the coordinates of vertex B be $(x_{B},y_{B})$ . We are given that vertex A is $(1,2)$ and the mid-point of side AB is $(5,-1)$ .

Using the mid-point formula, the coordinates of the mid-point are given by:

$(\frac{x_{A}+x_{B}}{2},\frac{y_{A}+y_{B}}{2})=(5,-1)$

By equating the $x$ and $y$ coordinates, we get:

$\frac{1+x_{B}}{2}=5⟹1+x_{B}=10⟹x_{B}=9$

$\frac{2+y_{B}}{2}=-1⟹2+y_{B}=-2⟹y_{B}=-4$

So, the coordinates of vertex B are $(9,-4)$ .

Let the coordinates of vertex C be $(x_{C},y_{C})$ . The centroid of a triangle with vertices $(x_{1},y_{1})$ , $(x_{2},y_{2})$ , and $(x_{3},y_{3})$ is given by the formula:

$(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}}{3},\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}}{3})$

We are given the centroid of triangle ABC is $(3,4)$ . Using the coordinates of vertices A, B, and C:

$\frac{1+9+x_{C}}{3}=3⟹10+x_{C}=9⟹x_{C}=-1$

$\frac{2+(-4)+y_{C}}{3}=4⟹-2+y_{C}=12⟹y_{C}=14$

So, the coordinates of vertex C are $(-1,14)$ .

The circumcenter of a triangle is a point that is equidistant from all three of its vertices. Let the given circumcenter be marked as $O(\alpha,\beta)$ . Therefore, we have:

$OA=OB=OC⟹OA^{2}=OB^{2}=OC^{2}$

Using the distance formula, we will write the equations for the squares of the distances:

$OA^{2}=(\alpha-1)^{2}+(\beta-2)^{2}=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-2\alpha-4\beta+5$

$OB^{2}=(\alpha-9)^{2}+(\beta+4)^{2}=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-18\alpha+8\beta+97$

$OC^{2}=(\alpha+1)^{2}+(\beta-14)^{2}=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+2\alpha-28\beta+197$

Now, equating $OA^{2}=OB^{2}$ :

$\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-2\alpha-4\beta+5=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-18\alpha+8\beta+97$

$16\alpha-12\beta=92$

Dividing the entire equation by 4 gives our first linear equation:

$4\alpha-3\beta=23\text{--- (Equation 1)}$

Next, equating $OA^{2}=OC^{2}$ :

$\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-2\alpha-4\beta+5=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+2\alpha-28\beta+197$

$-4\alpha+24\beta=192$

Dividing this equation by -4 gives our second linear equation:

$\alpha-6\beta=-48⟹\alpha=6\beta-48\text{--- (Equation 2)}$

Substitute the expression for $\alpha$ from Equation 2 into Equation 1:

$4(6\beta-48)-3\beta=23$

$24\beta-192-3\beta=23$

$21\beta-192=23$

$21\beta=215⟹\beta=\frac{215}{21}$

Now, substitute the value of $\beta$ back into Equation 2 to find $\alpha$ :

$\alpha=6(\frac{215}{21})-48$

$\alpha=\frac{1290}{21}-\frac{1008}{21}$

$\alpha=\frac{282}{21}$

The problem asks for the value of $21(\alpha+\beta)$ . We can simply plug in our values:

$21(\alpha+\beta)=21(\frac{282}{21}+\frac{215}{21})$

$21(\alpha+\beta)=282+215=497$

Option C is the correct answer.

solution : $A(1,0),B(2,-1)$ and $C(\frac{7}{3},\frac{4}{3})$

equation of line AB using two point form

$\begin{aligned} & y-0=\frac{0-(-1)}{1-2}(x-1) \\ & y=-x+1 \\ & L_{1}:x+y-1=0 \end{aligned}$

similarly equation of line $BC$ .

$\begin{aligned} & y+1=\frac{\frac{4}{3}-(-1)}{\frac{7}{3}-2}(x-2) \\ & y+1=\frac{7/3}{1/3}(x-2) \\ & y=7x-14-1 \\ & L_{2}:7x-y-15=0 \end{aligned}$

from graph ( 2,0 ) lies in the region of $\angleABC$ .

calculating $L_{1}(2,0) \cdot L_{2}(2,0)$

$(2+0-1) \cdot (7 \times 2-0-15)=1 \cdot (-1)=-1$

equation of angular bisector of $\angleABC$ is given as

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{x+y-1}{\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}}}= \pm \frac{7x-y-15}{\sqrt{7^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\ & \frac{x+y-1}{\sqrt{2}}= \pm \frac{7x-y-15}{\sqrt{50}} \\ & 5x+5y-5= \pm (7x-y-15) \end{aligned}$

since $L_{1}(2,0) \cdot L_{2}(2,0)$ is negative so equation of $\angleABC$ bisector in the region $(2,0)$ can be

find using negative sign from equation (1)

$\begin{aligned} & 5x+5y-5=-(7x-y-15) \\ & 5x+5y-5+7x-y-15=0 \\ & 12x+4y-20=0 \end{aligned}$

$3x+y=5$ comparing with bisector $\alpha x+\beta y=5$ .

$\alpha=3$ and $\beta=1$

$\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=9+1=10$ .

questions.question_text: Let the distance between two parallel lines be 5 units and a point $P$ lie between the lines at a unit distance from one of them. An equilateral triangle $PQR$ is formed such that $Q$ lies on one of the parallel lines, while R lies on the other. Then $(QR)^{2}$ is equal to _________.
questions.question_html: Let the distance between two parallel lines be 5 units and a point $P$ lie between the lines at a unit distance from one of them. An equilateral triangle $PQR$ is formed such that $Q$ lies on one of the parallel lines, while R lies on the other. Then $(QR)^{2}$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanation_text: We set up a coordinate system so that the two parallel lines are given by $y=0\text{and}y=5,$ since their distance is 5 units. Choose point $P=(0,1)$ so that the distance from $P$ to the line $y=0$ is 1 unit (and its distance to the line $y=5$ is 4 units). Let point $Q=(a,0)$ be on the line $y=0$ , and let point $R=(b,5)$ be on the line $y=5$ . Since triangle $PQR$ is equilateral with side length $s$ , we require: $PQ=PR=QR=s.$ A convenient method is to “rotate” $Q$ about $P$ by an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to obtain $R$ . In complex-number (or vector) terms, if we translate so that $P$ is at the origin, then the rotation is given by $e^{i60^{\circ}}=cos60^{\circ}+isin60^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}+i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$ Thus, writing $Q$ in vector form relative to $P$ , we have $Q-P=(a,-1).$ Rotating this by $60^{\circ}$ gives $R-P=(acos60^{\circ}-(-1)sin60^{\circ},asin60^{\circ}+(-1)cos60^{\circ}).$ Substituting the values $cos60^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$ and $sin60^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ , we obtain $\begin{aligned} R-P & =(\frac{a}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}), \\ \text{so}R & =(\frac{a+\sqrt{3}}{2},1+\frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1}{2})=(\frac{a+\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{a\sqrt{3}+1}{2}). \end{aligned}$ Since $R$ lies on $y=5$ , its $y$ -coordinate must equal 5: $\frac{a\sqrt{3}+1}{2}=5.$ Solve for $a$ : $\begin{aligned} a\sqrt{3}+1 & =10, \\ a\sqrt{3} & =9, \\ a & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{3}}=3\sqrt{3}. \end{aligned}$ Now, the side length $s$ (which is the distance $PQ$ ) is given by $\begin{aligned} s^{2} & =PQ^{2}=(3\sqrt{3}-0)^{2}+(0-1)^{2} \\ & =(3\sqrt{3})^{2}+1^{2} \\ & =27+1 \\ & =28. \end{aligned}$ Thus, the square of side $QR$ is $(QR)^{2}=s^{2}=28.$
questions.explanation_html:
We set up a coordinate system so that the two parallel lines are given by

$y=0\text{and}y=5,$

since their distance is 5 units. Choose point

$P=(0,1)$

so that the distance from $P$ to the line $y=0$ is 1 unit (and its distance to the line $y=5$ is 4 units).

Let point

$Q=(a,0)$

be on the line $y=0$ , and let point

$R=(b,5)$

be on the line $y=5$ . Since triangle $PQR$ is equilateral with side length $s$ , we require:

$PQ=PR=QR=s.$

A convenient method is to “rotate” $Q$ about $P$ by an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to obtain $R$ . In complex-number (or vector) terms, if we translate so that $P$ is at the origin, then the rotation is given by

$e^{i60^{\circ}}=cos60^{\circ}+isin60^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}+i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$

Thus, writing $Q$ in vector form relative to $P$ , we have

$Q-P=(a,-1).$

Rotating this by $60^{\circ}$ gives

$R-P=(acos60^{\circ}-(-1)sin60^{\circ},asin60^{\circ}+(-1)cos60^{\circ}).$

Substituting the values $cos60^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$ and $sin60^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ , we obtain

$\begin{aligned} R-P & =(\frac{a}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}), \\ \text{so}R & =(\frac{a+\sqrt{3}}{2},1+\frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1}{2})=(\frac{a+\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{a\sqrt{3}+1}{2}). \end{aligned}$

Since $R$ lies on $y=5$ , its $y$ -coordinate must equal 5:

$\frac{a\sqrt{3}+1}{2}=5.$

Solve for $a$ :

$\begin{aligned} a\sqrt{3}+1 & =10, \\ a\sqrt{3} & =9, \\ a & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{3}}=3\sqrt{3}. \end{aligned}$

Now, the side length $s$ (which is the distance $PQ$ ) is given by

$\begin{aligned} s^{2} & =PQ^{2}=(3\sqrt{3}-0)^{2}+(0-1)^{2} \\ & =(3\sqrt{3})^{2}+1^{2} \\ & =27+1 \\ & =28. \end{aligned}$

Thus, the square of side $QR$ is

$(QR)^{2}=s^{2}=28.$

questions.question_html: Let ABC be the triangle such that the equations of lines AB and AC be $3y-x=2$ and $x+y=2$ , respectively, and the points B and C lie on $x$ -axis. If P is the orthocentre of the triangle ABC , then the area of the triangle PBC is equal to
questions.explanation_text: Equation of line $AB$ is $3y-x=2$ And $AC$ is $x+y=2$ In line $AB$ , When $y=0,x=-2$ $\therefore B(-2,0)$ In line $AC$ , When $y=0,x=2$ $\therefore C(2x,0)$ Equation of altitude of $BC$ , $Y=x+2$ Similarly, equation of altitude of $AB$ , $y=-3x+6$ $\therefore$ On solving, orthocentre $P(1,3)$ $\therefore ar(△PBC)=6$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of line $AB$ is $3y-x=2$

And $AC$ is $x+y=2$

In line $AB$ ,

When $y=0,x=-2$

$\therefore B(-2,0)$

In line $AC$ ,

When $y=0,x=2$

$\therefore C(2x,0)$

Equation of altitude of $BC$ ,

$Y=x+2$

Similarly, equation of altitude of $AB$ ,

$y=-3x+6$

$\therefore$ On solving, orthocentre $P(1,3)$

$\therefore ar(△PBC)=6$

questions.question_html: Let the area of the triangle formed by a straight line $L:x+by+c=0$ with co-ordinate axes be 48 square units. If the perpendicular drawn from the origin to the line L makes an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with the positive $x$ -axis, then the value of $b^{2}+c^{2}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & L:x+by+c=0 \\ & \because \frac{1}{2}|(-c) \cdot (\frac{-c}{b})|=48 \\ & \therefore |\frac{c^{2}}{b}|=96\text{..... (i)} \end{aligned}$ Slope of line $L=-\frac{1}{b}$ $\therefore$ Slope of line perpendicular to $L$ is $b$ . $\begin{aligned} & \therefore b=1 \\ & \therefore c^{2}=96 \\ & \therefore b^{2}+c^{2}=97 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & L:x+by+c=0 \\ & \because \frac{1}{2}|(-c) \cdot (\frac{-c}{b})|=48 \\ & \therefore |\frac{c^{2}}{b}|=96\text{..... (i)} \end{aligned}$

Slope of line $L=-\frac{1}{b}$

$\therefore$ Slope of line perpendicular to $L$ is $b$ .

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore b=1 \\ & \therefore c^{2}=96 \\ & \therefore b^{2}+c^{2}=97 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $R$ be the interior region between the lines $3x-y+1=0$ and $x+2y-5=0$ containing the origin. The set of all values of $a$ , for which the points $(a^{2},a+1)$ lie in $R$ , is :
questions.question_html: Let $R$ be the interior region between the lines $3x-y+1=0$ and $x+2y-5=0$ containing the origin. The set of all values of $a$ , for which the points $(a^{2},a+1)$ lie in $R$ , is :
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & P(a^{2},a+1) \\ & L_{1}=3x-y+1=0 \end{aligned}$ Origin and $P$ lies same side w.r.t. $L_{1}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow L_{1}(0) \cdot L_{1}(P)>0 \\ & \therefore 3(a^{2})-(a+1)+1>0 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 3a^{2}-a>0 \\ & a \in (-\infty,0)∪(\frac{1}{3},\infty)\text{..... (1)} \end{aligned}$ Let $L_{2}:x+2y-5=0$ Origin and $P$ lies same side w.r.t. $L_{2}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow L_{2}(0) \cdot L_{2}(P)>0 \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}+2(a+1)-5<0 \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}+2a-3<0 \\ & \Rightarrow (a+3)(a-1)<0 \end{aligned}$ $\therefore a \in (-3,1)\text{..... (2)}$ Intersection of (1) and (2) $a \in (-3,0)∪(\frac{1}{3},1)$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & P(a^{2},a+1) \\ & L_{1}=3x-y+1=0 \end{aligned}$

Origin and $P$ lies same side w.r.t. $L_{1}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow L_{1}(0) \cdot L_{1}(P)>0 \\ & \therefore 3(a^{2})-(a+1)+1>0 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 3a^{2}-a>0 \\ & a \in (-\infty,0)∪(\frac{1}{3},\infty)\text{..... (1)} \end{aligned}$

Let $L_{2}:x+2y-5=0$

Origin and $P$ lies same side w.r.t. $L_{2}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow L_{2}(0) \cdot L_{2}(P)>0 \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}+2(a+1)-5<0 \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}+2a-3<0 \\ & \Rightarrow (a+3)(a-1)<0 \end{aligned}$

$\therefore a \in (-3,1)\text{..... (2)}$

Intersection of (1) and (2)

$a \in (-3,0)∪(\frac{1}{3},1)$

questions.question_html: If the orthocentre of the triangle formed by the lines $2x+3y-1=0,x+2y-1=0$ and $ax+by-1=0$ , is the centroid of another triangle, whose circumcentre and orthocentre respectively are $(3,4)$ and $(-6,-8)$ , then the value of $|a-b|$ is _________.
questions.explanation_text: Let circumcentre, orthocentre and centroid of a triangle $PQR$ are $C_{1},H_{1}$ and $G_{1}$ respectively $\Rightarrow G_{1} \equiv (0,0)$ orthocentre of $△ABC$ is $(0,0)$ $\begin{aligned} & m_{AH_{2}}=+\frac{b}{a} \Rightarrow a+b=0 \\ & \text{eq}^{\text{n}}\text{of lines}H_{2}C\text{is}y=\frac{3}{2}x \\ & \Rightarrow \text{point}C \equiv (\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{8})\text{lies on}ax+by-1=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{a}{4}+\frac{3}{8}b-1=0 \Rightarrow \frac{a}{4}-\frac{3}{8}a-1=0 \\ & \Rightarrow a=-8,b=8 \\ & |a-b|=16 \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow G_{1} \equiv (0,0)$ orthocentre of $△ABC$ is $(0,0)$

$\begin{aligned} & m_{AH_{2}}=+\frac{b}{a} \Rightarrow a+b=0 \\ & \text{eq}^{\text{n}}\text{of lines}H_{2}C\text{is}y=\frac{3}{2}x \\ & \Rightarrow \text{point}C \equiv (\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{8})\text{lies on}ax+by-1=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{a}{4}+\frac{3}{8}b-1=0 \Rightarrow \frac{a}{4}-\frac{3}{8}a-1=0 \\ & \Rightarrow a=-8,b=8 \\ & |a-b|=16 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: If the sum of squares of all real values of $\alpha$ , for which the lines $2x-y+3=0,6x+3y+1=0$ and $\alpha x+2y-2=0$ do not form a triangle is $p$ , then the greatest integer less than or equal to $p$ is _________.
questions.question_html: If the sum of squares of all real values of $\alpha$ , for which the lines $2x-y+3=0,6x+3y+1=0$ and $\alpha x+2y-2=0$ do not form a triangle is $p$ , then the greatest integer less than or equal to $p$ is _________.
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & 2x-y+3=0 \\ & 6x+3y+1=0 \\ & \alpha x+2y-2=0 \end{aligned}$ Will not form a $\Delta$ if $\alpha x+2y-2=0$ is concurrent with $2x-y+3=0$ and $6x+3y+1=0$ or parallel to either of them so Case-1: Concurrent lines $|\begin{aligned} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 6 & 3 & 1 \\ \alpha & 2 & -2 \end{aligned}|=0 \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{4}{5}$ Case-2 : Parallel lines $\begin{aligned} & -\frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{-6}{3}\text{or}-\frac{\alpha}{2}=2 \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=4\text{or}\alpha=-4 \\ & P=16+16+\frac{16}{25} \\ & [P]=[32+\frac{16}{25}]=32 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & 2x-y+3=0 \\ & 6x+3y+1=0 \\ & \alpha x+2y-2=0 \end{aligned}$

Will not form a $\Delta$ if $\alpha x+2y-2=0$ is concurrent with $2x-y+3=0$ and $6x+3y+1=0$ or parallel to either of them so

Case-1: Concurrent lines

$|\begin{aligned} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 6 & 3 & 1 \\ \alpha & 2 & -2 \end{aligned}|=0 \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{4}{5}$

Case-2 : Parallel lines

$\begin{aligned} & -\frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{-6}{3}\text{or}-\frac{\alpha}{2}=2 \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=4\text{or}\alpha=-4 \\ & P=16+16+\frac{16}{25} \\ & [P]=[32+\frac{16}{25}]=32 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: If the line segment joining the points $(5,2)$ and $(2,a)$ subtends an angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$ at the origin, then the absolute value of the product of all possible values of $a$ is :
questions.question_html: If the line segment joining the points $(5,2)$ and $(2,a)$ subtends an angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$ at the origin, then the absolute value of the product of all possible values of $a$ is :
questions.explanation_text: To solve this problem, we will use the concept of the slope and tangent of the angle subtended by the line segments at the origin. Given points: $(5,2)$ and $(2,a)$ The slope of the line joining the origin and $(5,2)$ is: $m_{1}=\frac{2-0}{5-0}=\frac{2}{5}$ The slope of the line joining the origin and $(2,a)$ is: $m_{2}=\frac{a-0}{2-0}=\frac{a}{2}$ The line segment joining these points subtends an angle $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$ at the origin. According to the tangent formula for the angle between two lines: $tan\theta=|\frac{m_{2}-m_{1}}{1+m_{1}m_{2}}|$ Here, $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$ so, $tan(\frac{\pi}{4})=1$ . Therefore, $1=|\frac{\frac{a}{2}-\frac{2}{5}}{1+(\frac{2}{5} \cdot \frac{a}{2})}|$ This simplifies to: $1=|\frac{\frac{5a-4}{10}}{1+\frac{2a}{10}}|$ Multiplying both the numerator and denominator by 10 to simplify: $1=|\frac{5a-4}{10+2a}|$ This leads to two equations due to the absolute value: 1. $5a-4=10+2a$ $3a=14$ $a=\frac{14}{3}$ 2. $5a-4=-(10+2a)$ $5a-4=-10-2a$ $7a=-6$ $a=-\frac{6}{7}$ Thus, the possible values of $a$ are $\frac{14}{3}$ and $-\frac{6}{7}$ . The product of these values is: $|\frac{14}{3} \times -\frac{6}{7}|$ $=|-\frac{84}{21}|$ $=|-4|$ $=4$ Therefore, the absolute value of the product of all possible values of $a$ is 4. Answer: Option A
questions.explanation_html:
To solve this problem, we will use the concept of the slope and tangent of the angle subtended by the line segments at the origin.

Given points: $(5,2)$ and $(2,a)$

The slope of the line joining the origin and $(5,2)$ is:

$m_{1}=\frac{2-0}{5-0}=\frac{2}{5}$

The slope of the line joining the origin and $(2,a)$ is:

$m_{2}=\frac{a-0}{2-0}=\frac{a}{2}$

The line segment joining these points subtends an angle $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$ at the origin.

According to the tangent formula for the angle between two lines:

$tan\theta=|\frac{m_{2}-m_{1}}{1+m_{1}m_{2}}|$

Here, $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$ so, $tan(\frac{\pi}{4})=1$ . Therefore,

$1=|\frac{\frac{a}{2}-\frac{2}{5}}{1+(\frac{2}{5} \cdot \frac{a}{2})}|$

This simplifies to:

$1=|\frac{\frac{5a-4}{10}}{1+\frac{2a}{10}}|$

Multiplying both the numerator and denominator by 10 to simplify:

$1=|\frac{5a-4}{10+2a}|$

This leads to two equations due to the absolute value:

1. $5a-4=10+2a$

$3a=14$ $a=\frac{14}{3}$

2. $5a-4=-(10+2a)$

$5a-4=-10-2a$ $7a=-6$ $a=-\frac{6}{7}$

Thus, the possible values of $a$ are $\frac{14}{3}$ and $-\frac{6}{7}$ .

The product of these values is:

$|\frac{14}{3} \times -\frac{6}{7}|$ $=|-\frac{84}{21}|$ $=|-4|$ $=4$

Therefore, the absolute value of the product of all possible values of $a$ is 4.

Answer: Option A

questions.question_html: The lines $L_{1},L_{2},\dots,L_{20}$ are distinct. For $n=1,2,3,\dots,10$ all the lines $L_{2n-1}$ are parallel to each other and all the lines $L_{2n}$ pass through a given point $P$ . The maximum number of points of intersection of pairs of lines from the set ${L_{1},L_{2},\dots,L_{20}}$ is equal to ___________.
questions.explanation_text: To find the maximum number of points of intersection of pairs of lines from the given set, we need to consider how the lines are arranged based on the given conditions. Firstly, there are 10 lines ( $L_{1},L_{3},...,L_{19}$ ) that are parallel to each other. Since parallel lines do not intersect with each other, these 10 lines will not contribute to the number of intersection points among themselves. Secondly, there are 10 lines ( $L_{2},L_{4},...,L_{20}$ ) that all pass through a given point $P$ . Although these lines intersect at $P$ , they only contribute one unique point of intersection to the total count. To calculate the maximum number of intersection points, we need to consider the total number of ways to pick pairs of lines from the 20 lines available without restrictions, then subtract the combinations that do not result in intersections, which includes the combinations of parallel lines among themselves and the concurrent lines through point $P$ . This calculation is represented as: $Total=^{20}C_{2}-^{10}C_{2}-^{10}C_{2}+1$ Here, $^{20}C_{2}$ calculates the total number of ways to pick any two lines out of 20, which includes intersecting and non-intersecting lines. $^{10}C_{2}$ is subtracted twice: once for the set of parallel lines ( $L_{1},L_{3},...,L_{19}$ ) that don't intersect among themselves and once more for the set of concurrent lines ( $L_{2},L_{4},...,L_{20}$ ) intersecting only at point $P$ . Since all the concurrent lines intersect at the same point, we add 1 back to include this intersection point. Carrying out this calculation gives us the total number of distinct intersection points as $101$ .

questions.question_html: Let a ray of light passing through the point $(3,10)$ reflects on the line $2x+y=6$ and the reflected ray passes through the point $(7,2)$ . If the equation of the incident ray is $ax+by+1=0$ , then $a^{2}+b^{2}+3ab$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanation_text: Equation of incident ray : $ax+by+1=0$ Using mirror image, $\frac{m-7}{2}=\frac{n-2}{1}=\frac{-2(14+2-6)}{5}$ $\begin{aligned} \frac{m-7}{2}=-4 & n-2=-4 \\ m=-8+7 & n=-2 \\ m=-1 & \end{aligned}$ $^{∗}$ Note: It can be observed from diagram $A,P,B$ ' are collinear. Equation of Incident Ray, Using two-point form, $\begin{aligned} & (y-10)=\frac{10+2}{3+1}(x-3) \\ & (y-10)=\frac{12}{4}(x-3) \\ & y-10=+3(x-3) \\ & y-10=+3x-9 \\ & 3x-y+1=0 \end{aligned}$ On comparing, $\begin{aligned} & a=3 \\ & b=-1 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of incident ray : $ax+by+1=0$

Using mirror image,

$\frac{m-7}{2}=\frac{n-2}{1}=\frac{-2(14+2-6)}{5}$

$\begin{aligned} \frac{m-7}{2}=-4 & n-2=-4 \\ m=-8+7 & n=-2 \\ m=-1 & \end{aligned}$

$^{∗}$ Note: It can be observed from diagram $A,P,B$ ' are collinear.

Equation of Incident Ray,

Using two-point form,

$\begin{aligned} & (y-10)=\frac{10+2}{3+1}(x-3) \\ & (y-10)=\frac{12}{4}(x-3) \\ & y-10=+3(x-3) \\ & y-10=+3x-9 \\ & 3x-y+1=0 \end{aligned}$

On comparing,

$\begin{aligned} & a=3 \\ & b=-1 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $C(\alpha,\beta)$ be the circumcenter of the triangle formed by the lines $4x+3y=69$ $4y-3x=17$ , and $x+7y=61$ . Then $(\alpha-\beta)^{2}+\alpha+\beta$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
Let $C(\alpha,\beta)$ be the circumcenter of the triangle formed by the lines

$4x+3y=69$

$4y-3x=17$ , and

$x+7y=61$ .

Then $(\alpha-\beta)^{2}+\alpha+\beta$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: We have, $\begin{aligned} & 4x+3y=69.......(i) \\ \\ & 4y-3x=17.......(ii) \\ \\ & x+7y=61.......(iii) \end{aligned}$ On solving (i) and (iii), we get, $\begin{aligned} & x=12,\text{and}y=7 \\ \\ & \text{So,}A \equiv (12,7) \end{aligned}$ On solving (ii) and (iii), we get, $\begin{aligned} & x=5\text{and}y=8 \\ \\ & \text{So, B} \equiv (5,8) \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Hence, circumcentre} \equiv (\frac{12+5}{2},\frac{7+8}{2}) \\ \\ & \equiv (\frac{17}{2},\frac{15}{2}) \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \alpha=\frac{17}{2},\beta=\frac{15}{2} \\ \\ & \therefore (\alpha-\beta)^{2}+(\alpha+\beta)=(\frac{17}{2}-\frac{15}{2})^{2}+(\frac{17}{2}+\frac{15}{2}) \\ \\ & =(1)^{2}+(16)=17 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
We have,

$\begin{aligned} & 4x+3y=69.......(i) \\ \\ & 4y-3x=17.......(ii) \\ \\ & x+7y=61.......(iii) \end{aligned}$

On solving (i) and (iii), we get,

$\begin{aligned} & x=12,\text{and}y=7 \\ \\ & \text{So,}A \equiv (12,7) \end{aligned}$


On solving (ii) and (iii), we get,

$\begin{aligned} & x=5\text{and}y=8 \\ \\ & \text{So, B} \equiv (5,8) \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Hence, circumcentre} \equiv (\frac{12+5}{2},\frac{7+8}{2}) \\ \\ & \equiv (\frac{17}{2},\frac{15}{2}) \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \alpha=\frac{17}{2},\beta=\frac{15}{2} \\ \\ & \therefore (\alpha-\beta)^{2}+(\alpha+\beta)=(\frac{17}{2}-\frac{15}{2})^{2}+(\frac{17}{2}+\frac{15}{2}) \\ \\ & =(1)^{2}+(16)=17 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: If the line $l_{1}:3y-2x=3$ is the angular bisector of the lines $l_{2}:x-y+1=0$ and $l_{3}:\alpha x+\beta y+17=0$ , then $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-\alpha-\beta$ is equal to _________.
questions.question_html: If the line $l_{1}:3y-2x=3$ is the angular bisector of the lines $l_{2}:x-y+1=0$ and $l_{3}:\alpha x+\beta y+17=0$ , then $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-\alpha-\beta$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & L_{1}:3y-2x=3 \\ \\ & L_{2}:x-y+1=0 \\ \\ & L_{3}:\alpha x+\beta y+17=0 \end{aligned}$ Point of intersection of $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ is $(0,1)$ , should lie on $L_{3} \Rightarrow \beta=-17$ Any point, say $(\frac{-3}{2},0)$ on $L_{1}$ should be equidistant from the lines $L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow |\frac{\frac{-3}{2}-0+1}{\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}}}|=|\frac{\frac{-3\alpha}{2}+0+17}{\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+(-17)^{2}}}| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (\alpha-7)(\alpha-17)=0 \end{aligned}$ For $\alpha=17,L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$ coincides $\Rightarrow \alpha=7$ $\begin{aligned} \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-\alpha-\beta & =(7)^{2}+(-17)^{2}-7+17 \\ \\ & =348 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & L_{1}:3y-2x=3 \\ \\ & L_{2}:x-y+1=0 \\ \\ & L_{3}:\alpha x+\beta y+17=0 \end{aligned}$

Point of intersection of $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ is $(0,1)$ , should lie on $L_{3} \Rightarrow \beta=-17$

Any point, say $(\frac{-3}{2},0)$ on $L_{1}$ should be equidistant from the lines $L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow |\frac{\frac{-3}{2}-0+1}{\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}}}|=|\frac{\frac{-3\alpha}{2}+0+17}{\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+(-17)^{2}}}| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (\alpha-7)(\alpha-17)=0 \end{aligned}$

For $\alpha=17,L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$ coincides $\Rightarrow \alpha=7$

$\begin{aligned} \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-\alpha-\beta & =(7)^{2}+(-17)^{2}-7+17 \\ \\ & =348 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: The straight lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ pass through the origin and trisect the line segment of the line L : $9x+5y=45$ between the axes. If $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are the slopes of the lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ , then the point of intersection of the line $y=(m_{1}+m_{2})x$ with L lies on :
questions.explanation_text: Given line $L:9x+5y=45$ ..........(i) Also given that $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are the slopes of the lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ , respectively. Let $A$ be the point of intersection of line $l_{1}$ and $L$ , then co-ordinates of $A$ are $(\frac{2 \times 5+1 \times 0}{2+1},\frac{2 \times 0+1 \times 9}{2+1})=(\frac{10}{3},3)$ And let $B$ be the point of intersection of line $l_{2}$ and $L$ , then co-ordinates of $B$ are $(\frac{1 \times 5+2 \times 0}{1+2},\frac{1 \times 0+2 \times 9}{1+2})=(\frac{5}{3},6)$ Now, slope of line $l_{1},(m_{1})=\frac{3-0}{\frac{10}{3}-0}=\frac{9}{10}$ and slope of lines $l_{2},(m_{2})=\frac{6-0}{\frac{5}{3}-0}=\frac{18}{5}$ $\begin{aligned} \therefore \text{line}y & =(m_{1}+m_{2})x \\ \\ & =(\frac{9}{10}+\frac{18}{5})x=\frac{45}{10}x=\frac{9}{2}x.......(ii) \end{aligned}$ Point of intersection of lines (i) and (ii) $\begin{aligned} & 9x+5(\frac{9}{2}x)=45 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x+\frac{5x}{2}=5 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{7x}{2}=5 \Rightarrow x=\frac{10}{7} \\ \\ & \text{and}y=\frac{9}{2} \times \frac{10}{7}=\frac{45}{7} \\ \\ & \therefore \text{Point of intersection}=(\frac{10}{7},\frac{45}{7}) \\ \\ & \text{lies on line}y-x=5 \end{aligned}$

Given line $L:9x+5y=45$ ..........(i)


Also given that $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are the slopes of the lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ , respectively.

Let $A$ be the point of intersection of line $l_{1}$ and $L$ , then

co-ordinates of $A$ are $(\frac{2 \times 5+1 \times 0}{2+1},\frac{2 \times 0+1 \times 9}{2+1})=(\frac{10}{3},3)$

And let $B$ be the point of intersection of line $l_{2}$ and $L$ , then

co-ordinates of $B$ are $(\frac{1 \times 5+2 \times 0}{1+2},\frac{1 \times 0+2 \times 9}{1+2})=(\frac{5}{3},6)$

Now, slope of line $l_{1},(m_{1})=\frac{3-0}{\frac{10}{3}-0}=\frac{9}{10}$

and slope of lines $l_{2},(m_{2})=\frac{6-0}{\frac{5}{3}-0}=\frac{18}{5}$

$\begin{aligned} \therefore \text{line}y & =(m_{1}+m_{2})x \\ \\ & =(\frac{9}{10}+\frac{18}{5})x=\frac{45}{10}x=\frac{9}{2}x.......(ii) \end{aligned}$

Point of intersection of lines (i) and (ii)

$\begin{aligned} & 9x+5(\frac{9}{2}x)=45 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x+\frac{5x}{2}=5 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{7x}{2}=5 \Rightarrow x=\frac{10}{7} \\ \\ & \text{and}y=\frac{9}{2} \times \frac{10}{7}=\frac{45}{7} \\ \\ & \therefore \text{Point of intersection}=(\frac{10}{7},\frac{45}{7}) \\ \\ & \text{lies on line}y-x=5 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $(\alpha,\beta)$ be the centroid of the triangle formed by the lines $15x-y=82,6x-5y=-4$ and $9x+4y=17$ . Then $\alpha+2\beta$ and $2\alpha-\beta$ are the roots of the equation :
questions.question_html: Let $(\alpha,\beta)$ be the centroid of the triangle formed by the lines $15x-y=82,6x-5y=-4$ and $9x+4y=17$ . Then $\alpha+2\beta$ and $2\alpha-\beta$ are the roots of the equation :
questions.explanation_text: Solve the equations $15x-y=82$ and $6x-5y=-4$ Multiply the first equation by 5 and the second by 1 and then subtract the second from the first: $75x-5y=410$ $6x-5y=-4$ Subtracting these gives $69x=414$ which leads to $x=6$ Substitute $x=6$ into the first equation to get $y=8$ So, the first vertex is $(6,8)$ . Solve the equations $15x-y=82$ and $9x+4y=17$ Multiply the first equation by 4 and the second by 1 and then add: $60x-4y=328$ $9x+4y=17$ Adding these gives $69x=345$ which leads to $x=5$ Substitute $x=5$ into the second equation to get $y=-7$ So, the second vertex is $(5,-7)$ . Solve the equations $6x-5y=-4$ and $9x+4y=17$ Multiply the first equation by 4 and the second by 5 and then add: $24x-20y=-16$ $45x+20y=85$ Adding these gives $69x=69$ which leads to $x=1$ Substitute $x=1$ into the first equation to get $y=2$ So, the third vertex is $(1,2)$ . So, the vertices of the triangle are $(6,8)$ , $(5,-7)$ , and $(1,2)$ . Now that we have the vertices of the triangle, we can find the centroid. The centroid $(\alpha,\beta)$ of a triangle with vertices $(x_{1},y_{1})$ , $(x_{2},y_{2})$ , and $(x_{3},y_{3})$ is given by : $\alpha=\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}}{3}$ , $\beta=\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}}{3}$ Substituting the coordinates of the vertices into these equations, we get: $\alpha=\frac{6+5+1}{3}=4$ , $\beta=\frac{8-7+2}{3}=1$ Then, we find $\alpha+2\beta$ and $2\alpha-\beta$ : $\alpha+2\beta=4+2(1)=62\alpha-\beta=2(4)-1=7$ So, $\alpha+2\beta=6$ and $2\alpha-\beta=7$ are the roots of the quadratic equation. We can write the quadratic equation as $x^{2}-(\alpha+2\beta+2\alpha-\beta)x+(\alpha+2\beta)(2\alpha-\beta)=0$ Substituting $\alpha=4$ , $\beta=1$ gives us: $x^{2}-13x+42=0$
questions.explanation_html:
1. Solve the equations $15x-y=82$ and $6x-5y=-4$

Multiply the first equation by 5 and the second by 1 and then subtract the second from the first:

$75x-5y=410$

$6x-5y=-4$

Subtracting these gives $69x=414$ which leads to $x=6$

Substitute $x=6$ into the first equation to get $y=8$

So, the first vertex is $(6,8)$ .

  1. Solve the equations $15x-y=82$ and $9x+4y=17$

Multiply the first equation by 4 and the second by 1 and then add:

$60x-4y=328$

$9x+4y=17$

Adding these gives $69x=345$ which leads to $x=5$

Substitute $x=5$ into the second equation to get $y=-7$

So, the second vertex is $(5,-7)$ .

  1. Solve the equations $6x-5y=-4$ and $9x+4y=17$

Multiply the first equation by 4 and the second by 5 and then add:

$24x-20y=-16$

$45x+20y=85$

Adding these gives $69x=69$ which leads to $x=1$

Substitute $x=1$ into the first equation to get $y=2$

So, the third vertex is $(1,2)$ .

So, the vertices of the triangle are $(6,8)$ , $(5,-7)$ , and $(1,2)$ .

Now that we have the vertices of the triangle, we can find the centroid. The centroid $(\alpha,\beta)$ of a triangle with vertices $(x_{1},y_{1})$ , $(x_{2},y_{2})$ , and $(x_{3},y_{3})$ is given by :

$\alpha=\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}}{3}$ ,

$\beta=\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}}{3}$

Substituting the coordinates of the vertices into these equations, we get:

$\alpha=\frac{6+5+1}{3}=4$ ,

$\beta=\frac{8-7+2}{3}=1$

Then, we find $\alpha+2\beta$ and $2\alpha-\beta$ :

$\alpha+2\beta=4+2(1)=62\alpha-\beta=2(4)-1=7$

So, $\alpha+2\beta=6$ and $2\alpha-\beta=7$ are the roots of the quadratic equation.

We can write the quadratic equation as

$x^{2}-(\alpha+2\beta+2\alpha-\beta)x+(\alpha+2\beta)(2\alpha-\beta)=0$

Substituting $\alpha=4$ , $\beta=1$ gives us:

$x^{2}-13x+42=0$

questions.explanation_text: Let point $P:(ℎ,k)$ $(ℎ-1)^{2}+(k-2)^{2}+(ℎ+2)^{2}+(k-1)^{2}=14$ $2ℎ^{2}+2k^{2}+2ℎ-6k-4=0$ Locus of $P:x^{2}+y^{2}+x-3y-2=0$ Intersection with x-axis, $x^{2}+x-2=0$ $\Rightarrow x=-2,1$ Intersection with y-axis, $y^{2}-3y-2=0$ $\Rightarrow y=\frac{3 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}$ Area of the quadrilateral ACBD is $=\frac{1}{2}(|x_{1}|+|x_{2}|)(|y_{1}|+|y_{2}|)$ $=\frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times \sqrt{17}=\frac{3\sqrt{17}}{2}$

questions.question_html: Let the area of the triangle with vertices A(1, $\alpha$ ), B( $\alpha$ , 0) and C(0, $\alpha$ ) be 4 sq. units. If the points ( $\alpha$ , $-$ $\alpha$ ), ( $-$ $\alpha$ , $\alpha$ ) and ( $\alpha$ 2, $\beta$ ) are collinear, then $\beta$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\because$ A(1, $\alpha$ ), B( $\alpha$ , 0) and C(0, $\alpha$ ) are the vertices of $\Delta$ ABC and area of $\Delta$ ABC = 4 $\therefore$ $|\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} 1 & \alpha & 1 \\ \alpha & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & \alpha & 1 \end{aligned}||=4$ $\Rightarrow |1(1-\alpha)-\alpha(\alpha)+\alpha^{2}|=8$ $\Rightarrow \alpha= \pm 8$ Now, $(\alpha,-\alpha),(-\alpha,\alpha)$ and $(\alpha^{2},\beta)$ are collinear $\therefore$ $|\begin{aligned} 8 & -8 & 1 \\ -8 & 8 & 1 \\ 64 & \beta & 1 \end{aligned}|=0=|\begin{aligned} -8 & 8 & 1 \\ 8 & -8 & 1 \\ 64 & \beta & 1 \end{aligned}|$ $\Rightarrow 8(8-\beta)+8(-8-64)+1(-8\beta-8 \times 64)=0$ $\Rightarrow 8-\beta-72-\beta-64=0$ $\Rightarrow \beta=-64$
questions.explanation_html:
$\because$ A(1, $\alpha$ ), B( $\alpha$ , 0) and C(0, $\alpha$ ) are the vertices of $\Delta$ ABC and area of $\Delta$ ABC = 4

$\therefore$ $|\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} 1 & \alpha & 1 \\ \alpha & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & \alpha & 1 \end{aligned}||=4$

$\Rightarrow |1(1-\alpha)-\alpha(\alpha)+\alpha^{2}|=8$

$\Rightarrow \alpha= \pm 8$

Now, $(\alpha,-\alpha),(-\alpha,\alpha)$ and $(\alpha^{2},\beta)$ are collinear

$\therefore$ $|\begin{aligned} 8 & -8 & 1 \\ -8 & 8 & 1 \\ 64 & \beta & 1 \end{aligned}|=0=|\begin{aligned} -8 & 8 & 1 \\ 8 & -8 & 1 \\ 64 & \beta & 1 \end{aligned}|$

$\Rightarrow 8(8-\beta)+8(-8-64)+1(-8\beta-8 \times 64)=0$

$\Rightarrow 8-\beta-72-\beta-64=0$

$\Rightarrow \beta=-64$

questions.question_html: A line, with the slope greater than one, passes through the point $A(4,3)$ and intersects the line $x-y-2=0$ at the point B. If the length of the line segment $AB$ is $\frac{\sqrt{29}}{3}$ , then $B$ also lies on the line :
questions.explanation_text: Let inclination of required line is $\theta$ , So the coordinates of point $B$ can be assumed as $(4-\frac{\sqrt{29}}{3}cos\theta,3-\frac{\sqrt{29}}{3}sin\theta)$ Which satisfices $x-y-2=0$ $4-\frac{\sqrt{29}}{3}cos\theta-3+\frac{\sqrt{29}}{3}sin\theta-2=0$ $sin\theta-cos\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt{29}}$ By squaring $sin2\theta=\frac{20}{29}=\frac{2tan\theta}{1+tan^{2}\theta}$ $tan\theta=\frac{5}{2}$ only (because slope is greater than 1 ) $sin\theta=\frac{5}{\sqrt{29}},cos\theta=\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}}$ Point $B:(\frac{10}{3},\frac{4}{3})$ Which also satisfies $x+2y=6$
questions.explanation_html:
Let inclination of required line is $\theta$ ,

So the coordinates of point $B$ can be assumed as

$(4-\frac{\sqrt{29}}{3}cos\theta,3-\frac{\sqrt{29}}{3}sin\theta)$

Which satisfices $x-y-2=0$

$4-\frac{\sqrt{29}}{3}cos\theta-3+\frac{\sqrt{29}}{3}sin\theta-2=0$

$sin\theta-cos\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt{29}}$

By squaring

$sin2\theta=\frac{20}{29}=\frac{2tan\theta}{1+tan^{2}\theta}$

$tan\theta=\frac{5}{2}$ only (because slope is greater than 1 )

$sin\theta=\frac{5}{\sqrt{29}},cos\theta=\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}}$

Point $B:(\frac{10}{3},\frac{4}{3})$

Which also satisfies $x+2y=6$

questions.explanation_text: Clearly $B$ is $(-\frac{3}{\sqrt{a}},+\sqrt{a})$ and $C$ is $(-\frac{3}{\sqrt{a}},-\sqrt{a})$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Area of}△ACD=\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} \frac{3}{\sqrt{a}} & \sqrt{a} & 1 \\ \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{a}} & -\sqrt{a} & 1 \\ \\ 3cos\theta & asin\theta & 1 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \Delta=|\begin{aligned} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{a}} & -\sqrt{a} & 1 \\ \\ 3cos\theta & asin\theta & 1 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \Delta=|3\sqrt{a}sin\theta+3\sqrt{a}cos\theta|=3\sqrt{a}|sin\theta+cos\theta| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \Delta_{max}=3\sqrt{a} \cdot \sqrt{2}=12 \Rightarrow a=(2\sqrt{2})^{2}=8 \end{aligned}$

If one vertex of the square is $(10(cos\alpha-sin\alpha),10(sin\alpha+cos\alpha))$ , where $\alpha \in (0,\frac{\pi}{2})$ and the equation of one diagonal is $(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)x+(sin\alpha+cos\alpha)y=10$ , then $72(sin^{4}\alpha+cos^{4}\alpha)+a^{2}-3a+13$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $m_{1},m_{2}$ be the slopes of two adjacent sides of a square of side a such that $a^{2}+11a+3(m_{1}^{2}+m_{2}^{2})=220$ . If one vertex of the square is $(10(cos\alpha-sin\alpha),10(sin\alpha+cos\alpha))$ , where $\alpha \in (0,\frac{\pi}{2})$ and the equation of one diagonal is $(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)x+(sin\alpha+cos\alpha)y=10$ , then $72(sin^{4}\alpha+cos^{4}\alpha)+a^{2}-3a+13$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: One vertex of square is $(10(cos\alpha-sin\alpha),10(sin\alpha+cos\alpha))$ and one of the diagonal is $(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)x+(sin\alpha+cos\alpha)y=10$ So the other diagonal can be obtained as $(cos\alpha+sin\alpha)x-(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)y=0$ So, the point of intersection of the diagonal will be (5( $cos\alpha-sin\alpha),5(cos\alpha+sin\alpha))$ . Therefore, the vertex opposite to the given vertex is $(0,0)$ . So, the diagonal length $=10\sqrt{2}$ Side length $(a)=10$ It is given that $a^{2}+11a+3(m_{1}^{2}+m_{2}^{2})=220$ $m_{1}^{2}+m_{2}^{2}=\frac{220-100-110}{3}=\frac{10}{3}$ and $m_{1}m_{2}=-1$ Slopes of the sides are tan $\alpha$ and $-cot\alpha$ $tan^{2}\alpha=3$ or $\frac{1}{3}$ $72(sin^{4}\alpha+cos^{4}\alpha)+a^{2}-3a+13$ $=72 \cdot \frac{tan^{4}\alpha+1}{(1+tan^{2}\alpha)^{2}}+a^{2}-3a+13=128$
questions.explanation_html:
One vertex of square is

$(10(cos\alpha-sin\alpha),10(sin\alpha+cos\alpha))$

and one of the diagonal is

$(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)x+(sin\alpha+cos\alpha)y=10$

So the other diagonal can be obtained as

$(cos\alpha+sin\alpha)x-(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)y=0$

So, the point of intersection of the diagonal will be

(5( $cos\alpha-sin\alpha),5(cos\alpha+sin\alpha))$ .

Therefore, the vertex opposite to the given vertex is $(0,0)$ .

So, the diagonal length $=10\sqrt{2}$

Side length $(a)=10$

It is given that

$a^{2}+11a+3(m_{1}^{2}+m_{2}^{2})=220$

$m_{1}^{2}+m_{2}^{2}=\frac{220-100-110}{3}=\frac{10}{3}$

and $m_{1}m_{2}=-1$

Slopes of the sides are tan $\alpha$ and $-cot\alpha$

$tan^{2}\alpha=3$ or $\frac{1}{3}$

$72(sin^{4}\alpha+cos^{4}\alpha)+a^{2}-3a+13$

$=72 \cdot \frac{tan^{4}\alpha+1}{(1+tan^{2}\alpha)^{2}}+a^{2}-3a+13=128$
