questions.question_text: Let $\alpha$ 1 , $\alpha$ 2 ( $\alpha$ 1 < $\alpha$ 2 ) be the values of $\alpha$ fo the points ( $\alpha$ , $-$ 3), (2, 0) and (1, $\alpha$ ) to be collinear. Then the equation of the line, passing through ( $\alpha$ 1 , $\alpha$ 2 ) and making an angle of $\frac{\pi}{3}$ with the positive direction of the x-axis, is :
questions.question_html: Let $\alpha$ 1, $\alpha$ 2 ( $\alpha$ 1 < $\alpha$ 2) be the values of $\alpha$ fo the points ( $\alpha$ , $-$ 3), (2, 0) and (1, $\alpha$ ) to be collinear. Then the equation of the line, passing through ( $\alpha$ 1, $\alpha$ 2) and making an angle of $\frac{\pi}{3}$ with the positive direction of the x-axis, is :
questions.explanation_text: Points A( $\alpha$ , $-$ 3), B(2, 0) and C(1, $\alpha$ ) are collinear. $\therefore$ Slope of AB = Slope of BC $\Rightarrow \frac{0+3}{2-\alpha}=\frac{\alpha-0}{1-2}$ $\Rightarrow -3=\alpha(2-\alpha)$ $\Rightarrow -3=2\alpha-\alpha^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}-2\alpha-3=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}-3\alpha+\alpha-3=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha(\alpha-3)+1(\alpha-3)=0$ $\Rightarrow (\alpha+1)(\alpha-3)=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=-1,3$ Given, $\alpha_{1}<\alpha_{2}$ $\therefore$ $\alpha_{1}=-1$ and $\alpha_{2}=3$ $\therefore$ $(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})=(-1,3)$ Now, equation of the line passing through ( $-$ 1, 3) and making angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$ with positive x-axis is $(y-y_{1})=m(x-x_{1})$ $\Rightarrow y-3=(tan\frac{\pi}{3})(x+1)$ $\Rightarrow y-3=\sqrt{3}(x+1)$ $\Rightarrow \sqrt{3}x-y+\sqrt{3}+3=0$
questions.explanation_html:
Points A( $\alpha$ , $-$ 3), B(2, 0) and C(1, $\alpha$ ) are collinear.

$\therefore$ Slope of AB = Slope of BC

$\Rightarrow \frac{0+3}{2-\alpha}=\frac{\alpha-0}{1-2}$

$\Rightarrow -3=\alpha(2-\alpha)$

$\Rightarrow -3=2\alpha-\alpha^{2}$

$\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}-2\alpha-3=0$

$\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}-3\alpha+\alpha-3=0$

$\Rightarrow \alpha(\alpha-3)+1(\alpha-3)=0$

$\Rightarrow (\alpha+1)(\alpha-3)=0$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=-1,3$

Given, $\alpha_{1}<\alpha_{2}$

$\therefore$ $\alpha_{1}=-1$ and $\alpha_{2}=3$

$\therefore$ $(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})=(-1,3)$

Now, equation of the line passing through ( $-$ 1, 3) and making angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$ with positive x-axis is

$(y-y_{1})=m(x-x_{1})$

$\Rightarrow y-3=(tan\frac{\pi}{3})(x+1)$

$\Rightarrow y-3=\sqrt{3}(x+1)$

$\Rightarrow \sqrt{3}x-y+\sqrt{3}+3=0$

taking +ve sign

taking $-$ ve sign

If the co-ordinates of the final position of the point P are $(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{7}{\sqrt{2}})$ , then the value of 2a + b is equal to :
questions.question_html:
The point P (a, b) undergoes the following three transformations successively :

(a) reflection about the line y = x.

(b) translation through 2 units along the positive direction of x-axis.

(c) rotation through angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$ about the origin in the anti-clockwise direction.

If the co-ordinates of the final position of the point P are $(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{7}{\sqrt{2}})$ , then the value of 2a + b is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Image of A(a, b) along y = x is B(b, a). Translating it 2 units it becomes C(b + 2, a). Now, applying rotation theorem $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{7}{\sqrt{2}}i=((b+2)+ai)(cos\frac{\pi}{4}+isin\frac{\pi}{4})$ $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{7}{\sqrt{2}}i=(\frac{b+2}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}})+i(\frac{b+2}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}})$ $\Rightarrow$ b $-$ a + 2 = $-$ 1 ......(i) and b + 2 + a = 7 ...... (ii) $\Rightarrow$ a = 4; b = 1 $\Rightarrow$ 2a + b = 9
questions.explanation_html:
Image of A(a, b) along y = x is B(b, a). Translating it 2 units it becomes C(b + 2, a).

Now, applying rotation theorem

$-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{7}{\sqrt{2}}i=((b+2)+ai)(cos\frac{\pi}{4}+isin\frac{\pi}{4})$

$-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{7}{\sqrt{2}}i=(\frac{b+2}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}})+i(\frac{b+2}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}})$

$\Rightarrow$ b $-$ a + 2 = $-$ 1 ......(i)

and b + 2 + a = 7 ...... (ii)

$\Rightarrow$ a = 4; b = 1

$\Rightarrow$ 2a + b = 9

questions.question_text: A square ABCD has all its vertices on the curve x 2 y 2 = 1. The midpoints of its sides also lie on the same curve. Then, the square of area of ABCD is _________.
questions.question_html: A square ABCD has all its vertices on the curve x2y2 = 1. The midpoints of its sides also lie on the same curve. Then, the square of area of ABCD is _________.
questions.explanation_text: x 2 y 2 = 1 $\Rightarrow$ y 2 = $\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ y = $\pm \frac{1}{x}$ Graph of this equation, $OA\perpOB$ $\Rightarrow (\frac{1}{p^{2}})(-\frac{1}{q^{2}})=-1$ $\Rightarrow p^{2}q^{2}=1$ $P(\frac{p+q}{2},\frac{\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}}{2})$ midpoint of AB lies On $x^{2}y^{2}=1$ $\Rightarrow (p+q)^{2}(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q})^{2}=16$ $\Rightarrow (p+q)^{2}(p-q)^{2}=16$ $\Rightarrow (p^{2}-q^{2})^{2}=16$ $\Rightarrow P^{2}-\frac{1}{P^{2}}= \pm 4$ $\Rightarrow p^{4} \pm 4p^{2}-1=0$ $\Rightarrow p^{2}=\frac{\pm 4 \pm \sqrt{20}}{2}= \pm 2 \pm \sqrt{5}$ $\Rightarrow p^{2}=2+\sqrt{5}$ or $-2+\sqrt{5}$ $OB^{2}=p^{2}+\frac{1}{p^{2}}=2+\sqrt{5}+\frac{1}{2+\sqrt{5}}$ or $-2+\sqrt{5}+\frac{1}{-2+\sqrt{5}}=2\sqrt{5}$ Area $=4(\frac{1}{2})(OA)(OB)=2(OB)^{2}=4\sqrt{5}$
questions.explanation_html:
x2y2 = 1

$\Rightarrow$ y2 = $\frac{1}{x^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ y = $\pm \frac{1}{x}$

Graph of this equation,

$OA\perpOB$

$\Rightarrow (\frac{1}{p^{2}})(-\frac{1}{q^{2}})=-1$

$\Rightarrow p^{2}q^{2}=1$

$P(\frac{p+q}{2},\frac{\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}}{2})$ midpoint of AB lies

On $x^{2}y^{2}=1$

$\Rightarrow (p+q)^{2}(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q})^{2}=16$

$\Rightarrow (p+q)^{2}(p-q)^{2}=16$

$\Rightarrow (p^{2}-q^{2})^{2}=16$

$\Rightarrow P^{2}-\frac{1}{P^{2}}= \pm 4$

$\Rightarrow p^{4} \pm 4p^{2}-1=0$

$\Rightarrow p^{2}=\frac{\pm 4 \pm \sqrt{20}}{2}= \pm 2 \pm \sqrt{5}$

$\Rightarrow p^{2}=2+\sqrt{5}$ or $-2+\sqrt{5}$

$OB^{2}=p^{2}+\frac{1}{p^{2}}=2+\sqrt{5}+\frac{1}{2+\sqrt{5}}$ or $-2+\sqrt{5}+\frac{1}{-2+\sqrt{5}}=2\sqrt{5}$

Area $=4(\frac{1}{2})(OA)(OB)=2(OB)^{2}=4\sqrt{5}$

questions.question_text: Let the points of intersections of the lines x $-$ y + 1 = 0, x $-$ 2y + 3 = 0 and 2x $-$ 5y + 11 = 0 are the mid points of the sides of a triangle $\Delta$ ABC. Then, the area of the $\Delta$ ABC is _____________.
questions.question_html: Let the points of intersections of the lines x $-$ y + 1 = 0, x $-$ 2y + 3 = 0 and 2x $-$ 5y + 11 = 0 are the mid points of the sides of a triangle $\Delta$ ABC. Then, the area of the $\Delta$ ABC is _____________.
questions.explanation_text: Intersection point of given lines are (1, 2), (7, 5), (2, 3) $\Delta=\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 7 & 5 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{aligned}|$ $=\frac{1}{2}[1(5-3)-2(7-2)+1(21-10)]$ $=\frac{1}{2}[2-10+11]$ $\Delta$ DEF $=\frac{1}{2}(3)=\frac{3}{2}$ $\Delta$ ABC = 4 $\Delta$ DEF $=4(\frac{3}{2})=6$
questions.explanation_html:
Intersection point of given lines are (1, 2), (7, 5), (2, 3)


$\Delta=\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 7 & 5 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{aligned}|$

$=\frac{1}{2}[1(5-3)-2(7-2)+1(21-10)]$

$=\frac{1}{2}[2-10+11]$

$\Delta$ DEF $=\frac{1}{2}(3)=\frac{3}{2}$

$\Delta$ ABC = 4 $\Delta$ DEF $=4(\frac{3}{2})=6$

If circumcentre of $\Delta$ ABC coincides with origin and its orthocentre lies on y-axis, then the value of $(\frac{cos3\alpha+cos3\beta+cos3\gamma}{cos\alpha cos\beta cos\gamma})^{2}$ is equal to ____________.
questions.question_html: Let tan $\alpha$ , tan $\beta$ and tan $\gamma$ ; $\alpha$ , $\beta$ , $\gamma$ $\ne$ $\frac{(2n-1)\pi}{2}$ , n $\in$ N be the slopes of three line segments OA, OB and OC, respectively, where O is origin. If circumcentre of $\Delta$ ABC coincides with origin and its orthocentre lies on y-axis, then the value of $(\frac{cos3\alpha+cos3\beta+cos3\gamma}{cos\alpha cos\beta cos\gamma})^{2}$ is equal to ____________.
questions.explanation_text: Since orthocentre and circumcentre both lies on y-axis. $\Rightarrow$ Centroid also lies on y-axis. $\Rightarrow$ $\sum cos\alpha=0$ cos $\alpha$ + cos $\beta$ + cos $\gamma$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ cos 3 $\alpha$ + cos 3 $\beta$ + cos 3 $\gamma$ = 3cos $\alpha$ cos $\beta$ cos $\gamma$ $\therefore$ $\frac{cos3\alpha+cos3\beta+cos3\gamma}{cos\alpha cos\beta cos\gamma}$ $=\frac{4(cos^{3}\alpha+cos^{3}\beta+cos^{3}\gamma)-3(cos\alpha+cos\beta+cos\gamma)}{cos\alpha cos\beta cos\gamma}=12$ then, $(\frac{cos3\alpha+cos3\beta+cos3\gamma}{cos\alpha cos\beta cos\gamma})^{2}=144$
questions.explanation_html:
Since orthocentre and circumcentre both lies on y-axis.

$\Rightarrow$ Centroid also lies on y-axis.

$\Rightarrow$ $\sum cos\alpha=0$

cos $\alpha$ + cos $\beta$ + cos $\gamma$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ cos3 $\alpha$ + cos3 $\beta$ + cos3 $\gamma$ = 3cos $\alpha$ cos $\beta$ cos $\gamma$

$\therefore$ $\frac{cos3\alpha+cos3\beta+cos3\gamma}{cos\alpha cos\beta cos\gamma}$

$=\frac{4(cos^{3}\alpha+cos^{3}\beta+cos^{3}\gamma)-3(cos\alpha+cos\beta+cos\gamma)}{cos\alpha cos\beta cos\gamma}=12$

then, $(\frac{cos3\alpha+cos3\beta+cos3\gamma}{cos\alpha cos\beta cos\gamma})^{2}=144$

and C on the ground. If P is the point of intersection of BC and AD, then the height of P (in m)
above the line AC is :
questions.question_html: Two vertical poles AB = 15 m and CD = 10 m are standing apart on a horizontal ground with points A and C on the ground. If P is the point of intersection of BC and AD, then the height of P (in m) above the line AC is :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of AD : $y=\frac{10}{a}x$ Equation of BC : $\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{15}=1$ $\Rightarrow \frac{ay}{10a}+\frac{y}{15}=1$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3y+2y}{30}=1$ $\Rightarrow y=6$ $\therefore$ y coordinate of point P = 6 = height of point P above the line AC.
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of AD : $y=\frac{10}{a}x$

Equation of BC : $\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{15}=1$

$\Rightarrow \frac{ay}{10a}+\frac{y}{15}=1$

$\Rightarrow \frac{3y+2y}{30}=1$

$\Rightarrow y=6$

$\therefore$ y coordinate of point P = 6 = height of point P above the line AC.

questions.question_html: Let two points be A(1, –1) and B(0, 2). If a point P(x', y') be such that the area of $\Delta$ PAB = 5 sq. units and it lies on the line, 3x + y – 4 $\lambda$ = 0, then a value of $\lambda$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Point P(x', y') lies on the line 3x + y – 4 $\lambda$ = 0 $\therefore$ 3x' + y' – 4 $\lambda$ = 0 Area of $\Delta$ PAB = 5 $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & x^{'} & y^{'} \end{aligned}|$ = $\pm$ 5 $\Rightarrow$ [(–2x') – (y' – 2) – (x')] = $\pm$ 10 $\Rightarrow$ – 3x' – y' + 2 = $\pm$ 10 $\Rightarrow$ 2 - 4 $\lambda$ = $\pm$ 10 $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = -2 or $\lambda$ = 3
questions.explanation_html:
Point P(x', y') lies on the line 3x + y – 4 $\lambda$ = 0

$\therefore$ 3x' + y' – 4 $\lambda$ = 0

Area of $\Delta$ PAB = 5

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & x^{'} & y^{'} \end{aligned}|$ = $\pm$ 5

$\Rightarrow$ [(–2x') – (y' – 2) – (x')] = $\pm$ 10

$\Rightarrow$ – 3x' – y' + 2 = $\pm$ 10

$\Rightarrow$ 2 - 4 $\lambda$ = $\pm$ 10

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = -2 or $\lambda$ = 3

questions.explanation_text: Slope of line y = x is 1 Line AB is perpendicular to line y = x so Slope of AB = -1 Also slope of AB = $\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2\alpha-\beta}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2\alpha-\beta}$ = -1 $\Rightarrow$ 3 $\alpha$ = 2 $\beta$ h = $\frac{2\alpha+\beta}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ 2h = $\frac{4\alpha+2\beta}{2}$ = $\frac{4\alpha+3\alpha}{2}$ = $\frac{7\alpha}{2}$ Also k = $\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ 2k = $\frac{5\alpha}{2}$ So $\frac{ℎ}{k}=\frac{7}{5}$ $\Rightarrow$ 5h = 7k $\Rightarrow$ 5x = 7y

questions.question_text: If the line, 2x - y + 3 = 0 is at a distance $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$ from the lines 4x - 2y + $\alpha$ = 0 and 6x - 3y + $\beta$ = 0, respectively, then the sum of all possible values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is :
questions.question_html:
If the line, 2x - y + 3 = 0 is at a distance
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$ from the lines 4x - 2y + $\alpha$ = 0
and 6x - 3y + $\beta$ = 0, respectively, then the sum of all possible values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Apply distance between parallel line formula $4x-2y+\alpha=0$ $4x-2y+6=0$ $|\frac{\alpha-6}{25}|=\frac{1}{55}$ $|\alpha-6|=2 \Rightarrow \alpha=8,4$ sum = 12 Again $6x-3y+\beta=0$ $6x-3y+9=0$ $|\frac{\beta-9}{3\sqrt{5}}|=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$ $|\beta-9|=6 \Rightarrow \beta=15,3$ sum = 18 $\therefore$ Sum of all values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is = 30
questions.explanation_html:
Apply distance between parallel line formula

$4x-2y+\alpha=0$

$4x-2y+6=0$

$|\frac{\alpha-6}{25}|=\frac{1}{55}$

$|\alpha-6|=2 \Rightarrow \alpha=8,4$

sum = 12

Again

$6x-3y+\beta=0$

$6x-3y+9=0$

$|\frac{\beta-9}{3\sqrt{5}}|=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$

$|\beta-9|=6 \Rightarrow \beta=15,3$

sum = 18

$\therefore$ Sum of all values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is = 30

If P is a Point inside the triangle ABC such that the triangles APC, APB and BPC have equal areas, then the length of the line segment PQ, where Q is the point $(-\frac{7}{6},-\frac{1}{3})$ , is ________.
questions.explanation_text: P is centroid of the triangle ABC. P = $(\frac{1+6+\frac{3}{2}}{3},\frac{0+2+6}{3})$ = $(\frac{17}{6},\frac{8}{3})$ Given Q $(-\frac{7}{6},-\frac{1}{3})$ . $\therefore$ PQ = $\sqrt{(\frac{24}{6})^{2}+(\frac{9}{3})^{2}}$ = 5

P = $(\frac{1+6+\frac{3}{2}}{3},\frac{0+2+6}{3})$

= $(\frac{17}{6},\frac{8}{3})$

Given Q $(-\frac{7}{6},-\frac{1}{3})$ .

$\therefore$ PQ = $\sqrt{(\frac{24}{6})^{2}+(\frac{9}{3})^{2}}$ = 5

equation of perpendicular bisector

for y intercept put x = 0

$y=\frac{7}{2}-(\frac{k^{2}-1}{2})=-4$

questions.question_text:
If the two lines x + (a – 1) y = 1 and
2x + a 2 y = 1 (a $\in$ R – {0, 1}) are perpendicular, then
the distance of their point of intersection from the
origin is :
questions.question_html: If the two lines x + (a – 1) y = 1 and 2x + a2y = 1 (a $\in$ R – {0, 1}) are perpendicular, then the distance of their point of intersection from the origin is :
questions.explanation_text: Line 1 : x + (a – 1) y = 1 Slope of this line (m 1 ) = $\frac{-1}{a-1}$ Line 2 : 2x + a 2 y = 1 Slope of this line (m 2 ) = $-\frac{2}{a^{2}}$ Line 1 and Line 2 are perpendicular to each other. $\therefore$ m 1 m 2 = -1 $\Rightarrow$ $(\frac{-1}{a-1})(-\frac{2}{a^{2}})=-1$ $\Rightarrow$ $a^{3}-a^{2}+2=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $(a+1)$ $(a^{2}-2a+2)$ = 0 $\therefore$ $a=-1$ So lines are Line 1 : x - 2y + 1 = 0 Line 2 : 2x + y - 1 = 0 Solving these equation we get point of intersection P $(\frac{3}{5},-\frac{1}{5})$ Now distance of P from origin OP = $\sqrt{(\frac{3}{5})^{2}+(-\frac{1}{5})^{2}}$ = $\sqrt{\frac{10}{25}}$ = $\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}$
questions.explanation_html:
Line 1 : x + (a – 1) y = 1

Slope of this line (m1) = $\frac{-1}{a-1}$

Line 2 : 2x + a2y = 1

Slope of this line (m2) = $-\frac{2}{a^{2}}$

Line 1 and Line 2 are perpendicular to each other.

$\therefore$ m1 m2 = -1

$\Rightarrow$ $(\frac{-1}{a-1})(-\frac{2}{a^{2}})=-1$

$\Rightarrow$ $a^{3}-a^{2}+2=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $(a+1)$ $(a^{2}-2a+2)$ = 0

$\therefore$ $a=-1$

So lines are

Line 1 : x - 2y + 1 = 0

Line 2 : 2x + y - 1 = 0

Solving these equation we get point of intersection

P $(\frac{3}{5},-\frac{1}{5})$

Now distance of P from origin

OP = $\sqrt{(\frac{3}{5})^{2}+(-\frac{1}{5})^{2}}$

= $\sqrt{\frac{10}{25}}$

= $\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}$

questions.question_text:
Suppose that the points (h,k), (1,2) and (–3,4) lie
on the line L 1 . If a line L 2 passing through the points
(h,k) and (4,3) is perpendicular to L 1 , then $\frac{k}{ℎ}$ equals :
questions.question_html: Suppose that the points (h,k), (1,2) and (–3,4) lie on the line L1 . If a line L2 passing through the points (h,k) and (4,3) is perpendicular to L1 , then $\frac{k}{ℎ}$ equals :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of line L 1 passing through points (1, 2) and (–3, 4) is : y - 2 = $(\frac{4-2}{-3-1})$ (x - 1) $\Rightarrow$ y - 2 = $-\frac{1}{2}$ (x - 1) $\Rightarrow$ 2y – 4 = –x + 1 $\Rightarrow$ x + 2y = 5 .......(L 1 ) Line L 1 passes through point (h, k). $\therefore$ h + 2k = 5 .......(1) Line L 2 is perpendicular to line L 1 . $\therefore$ Equation of line L 2 : 2x - y = $\lambda$ This line L 2 passes through point (4, 3). $\therefore$ 2(4) - 3 = $\lambda$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = 5 $\therefore$ Line L 2 : 2x - y = 5 L 2 also passes through (h, k) $\therefore$ 2h - k = 5 ............(2) Solving (1) and (2) we get, h = 3 and k = 1 $\therefore$ $\frac{k}{ℎ}=\frac{1}{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of line L1 passing through points (1, 2) and (–3, 4) is :

y - 2 = $(\frac{4-2}{-3-1})$ (x - 1)

$\Rightarrow$ y - 2 = $-\frac{1}{2}$ (x - 1)

$\Rightarrow$ 2y – 4 = –x + 1

$\Rightarrow$ x + 2y = 5 .......(L1)

Line L1 passes through point (h, k).

$\therefore$ h + 2k = 5 .......(1)

Line L2 is perpendicular to line L1.

$\therefore$ Equation of line L2 :

2x - y = $\lambda$

This line L2 passes through point (4, 3).

$\therefore$ 2(4) - 3 = $\lambda$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = 5

$\therefore$ Line L2 :

2x - y = 5

L2 also passes through (h, k)

$\therefore$ 2h - k = 5 ............(2)

Solving (1) and (2) we get,

h = 3 and k = 1

$\therefore$ $\frac{k}{ℎ}=\frac{1}{3}$

questions.question_html: Let the equations of two sides of a triangle be 3x $-$ 2y + 6 = 0 and 4x + 5y $-$ 20 = 0. If the orthocentre of this triangle is at (1, 1), then the equation of its third side is :
questions.explanation_text: 4x + 5y $-$ 20 = 0       . . .(1) 3x $-$ 2y + 6 = 0       . . . (2) orthocentre is (1, 1) line perpendicular to 4x + 5y $-$ 20 = 0 and passes through (1, 1) is (y $-$ 1) = $\frac{5}{4}$ (x $-$ 1) $\Rightarrow$ 5x $-$ 4y = 1       . . .(3) and line $\perp$ to 3x $-$ 2y + 6 = 0 and passes through (1, 1) y $-$ 1 = $-$ $\frac{2}{3}$ (x $-$ 1) $\Rightarrow$ 2x + 3y = 5       . . .(4) Solving (1) and (4) we get C $(\frac{35}{2},-10)$ Solving (2) and (3) we get A $(-13,\frac{-33}{2})$ Side BC is y + 10 = $\frac{\frac{-33}{2}+10}{-13-\frac{35}{2}}(x-\frac{35}{2})$ $\Rightarrow$ y + 10 = $\frac{13}{61}(x-\frac{35}{2})$ $\Rightarrow$ 26x $-$ 122y $-$ 1675 = 0

$\Rightarrow$   5x $-$ 4y = 1       . . .(3)

and line $\perp$ to 3x $-$ 2y + 6 = 0

and passes through (1, 1)

$\Rightarrow$   2x + 3y = 5       . . .(4)

Solving (2) and (3) we get A $(-13,\frac{-33}{2})$

Side BC is y + 10 = $\frac{\frac{-33}{2}+10}{-13-\frac{35}{2}}(x-\frac{35}{2})$

options.label: B

questions.explanation_html:

x cos $\theta$ + y sin $\theta$ = p

$\Rightarrow$ x cos (75o) + y sin (75o) = 4

$\Rightarrow$ $x(\sqrt{3}-1)+y(\sqrt{3}+1)=8\sqrt{2}$

questions.question_text:
Slope of a line passing through P(2, 3) and
intersecting the line, x + y = 7 at a distance of
4 units from P, is :
questions.question_html: Slope of a line passing through P(2, 3) and intersecting the line, x + y = 7 at a distance of 4 units from P, is :
questions.explanation_text: We know parametric form of straight line is $\frac{x-x_{1}}{cos\theta}=\frac{y-y_{1}}{sin\theta}=r$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{x-2}{cos\theta}=\frac{y-3}{sin\theta}=4$ $\therefore$ x = 4 + 2cos $\theta$ y = 4 + 3sin $\theta$ $\therefore$ Point A = (4 + 2cos $\theta$ , 4 + 3sin $\theta$ ) Point A lies on line x + y = 7, $\therefore$ (4 + 2cos $\theta$ ) + (4 + 3sin $\theta$ ) = 7 $\Rightarrow$ sin $\theta$ + cos $\theta$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $sin^{2}\theta+cos^{2}\theta$ + 2sin $\theta$ cos $\theta$ = $\frac{1}{4}$ $\Rightarrow$ 1 + sin 2 $\theta$ = $\frac{1}{4}$ $\Rightarrow$ sin 2 $\theta$ = $-\frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{2tan\theta}{1+tan^{2}\theta}$ = $-\frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow$ 3tan 2 $\theta$ + 8tan $\theta$ + 3 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ tan $\theta$ = $\frac{-8 \pm 2\sqrt{7}}{6}$ So slope = $\frac{-8 \pm 2\sqrt{7}}{6}$ By checking each options, Slope = $\frac{1-\sqrt{7}}{1+\sqrt{7}}$ As $\frac{1-\sqrt{7}}{1+\sqrt{7}}$ = $\frac{(1-\sqrt{7})^{2}}{1-7}$ = $\frac{8-2\sqrt{7}}{-6}$ = $\frac{-8+2\sqrt{7}}{6}$
questions.explanation_html:
We know parametric form of straight line is

$\frac{x-x_{1}}{cos\theta}=\frac{y-y_{1}}{sin\theta}=r$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{x-2}{cos\theta}=\frac{y-3}{sin\theta}=4$

$\therefore$ x = 4 + 2cos $\theta$

y = 4 + 3sin $\theta$

$\therefore$ Point A = (4 + 2cos $\theta$ , 4 + 3sin $\theta$ )

Point A lies on line x + y = 7,

$\therefore$ (4 + 2cos $\theta$ ) + (4 + 3sin $\theta$ ) = 7

$\Rightarrow$ sin $\theta$ + cos $\theta$ = $\frac{1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $sin^{2}\theta+cos^{2}\theta$ + 2sin $\theta$ cos $\theta$ = $\frac{1}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ 1 + sin 2 $\theta$ = $\frac{1}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ sin 2 $\theta$ = $-\frac{3}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{2tan\theta}{1+tan^{2}\theta}$ = $-\frac{3}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ 3tan2 $\theta$ + 8tan $\theta$ + 3 = 0

$\Rightarrow$ tan $\theta$ = $\frac{-8 \pm 2\sqrt{7}}{6}$

So slope = $\frac{-8 \pm 2\sqrt{7}}{6}$

By checking each options,

Slope = $\frac{1-\sqrt{7}}{1+\sqrt{7}}$

As $\frac{1-\sqrt{7}}{1+\sqrt{7}}$ = $\frac{(1-\sqrt{7})^{2}}{1-7}$ = $\frac{8-2\sqrt{7}}{-6}$ = $\frac{-8+2\sqrt{7}}{6}$

questions.question_text: In a triangle ABC, coordinates of A are (1, 2) and the equations of the medians through B and C are respectively, x + y = 5 and x = 4. Then area of $\Delta$ ABC (in sq. units) is :
questions.question_html: In a triangle ABC, coordinates of A are (1, 2) and the equations of the medians through B and C are respectively, x + y = 5 and x = 4. Then area of $\Delta$ ABC (in sq. units) is :
questions.explanation_text: Median through C is x = 4 So the coordinate of C is 4. Let C = (4, y), then the midpoint of A(1, 2) and C(4, y) is D which lies on the median through B. $\therefore$ D = $(\frac{1+4}{2},\frac{2+y}{2})$ Now, $\frac{1+4+2+y}{2}$ = 5 $\Rightarrow$ y = 3. So, C $\equiv$ (4, 3). The centroid of the triangle is the intersection of the mesians, Here the medians x = 4 and x + 4 and x + y = 5 intersect at G (4, 1). The area of triangle $\Delta$ ABC = 3 $\times$ $\Delta$ AGC = 3 $\times$ $\frac{1}{2}$ [1(1 $-$ 3) + 4(3 $-$ 2) + 4(2 $-$ 1)] = 9.

questions.question_text: The foot of the perpendicular drawn from the origin, on the line, 3x + y = $\lambda$ ( $\lambda$ $\ne$ 0) is P. If the line meets x-axis at A and y-axis at B, then the ratio BP : PA is :
questions.question_html: The foot of the perpendicular drawn from the origin, on the line, 3x + y = $\lambda$ ( $\lambda$ $\ne$ 0) is P. If the line meets x-axis at A and y-axis at B, then the ratio BP : PA is :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of the line, which is perpendicular to the line, 3x + y = $\lambda$ ( $\lambda$ $\ne$ 0) and passing through origin , is given by $\frac{x-0}{3}=\frac{y-0}{1}=r$ For foot of perpendicular r = $\frac{-((3 \times 0)+(1 \times 0)-\lambda)}{3^{2}+1^{2}}$ = $\frac{\lambda}{10}$ So, foot of perpendicular P = $(\frac{3\lambda}{10},\frac{\lambda}{10})$ Given the line meets X-axis where y = 0, so 3x + 0 = $\lambda$ $\Rightarrow$ x = $\frac{\lambda}{3}$ Hence, coordinates of A = $(\frac{\lambda}{3},0)$ and meets Y-axis at B = (0, $\lambda$ ) So, BP = $\sqrt{(\frac{3\lambda}{10})^{2}+(\frac{\lambda}{10}-\lambda)^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ BP = $\sqrt{\frac{9\lambda^{2}}{100}+\frac{81\lambda^{2}}{100}}$ = BP = $\sqrt{\frac{90\lambda^{2}}{100}}$ Now, PA = $\sqrt{(\frac{\lambda}{3}-\frac{3\lambda}{10})^{2}+(0-\frac{\lambda}{10})^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ PA = $\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{2}}{900}+\frac{\lambda^{2}}{100}} \Rightarrow PA$ = $\sqrt{\frac{10\lambda^{2}}{900}}$ Therefore BP : PA = 9 : 1

So, foot of perpendicular P = $(\frac{3\lambda}{10},\frac{\lambda}{10})$

$\Rightarrow$ x = $\frac{\lambda}{3}$

Hence, coordinates of A = $(\frac{\lambda}{3},0)$ and meets

Y-axis at B = (0, $\lambda$ )

So, BP = $\sqrt{(\frac{3\lambda}{10})^{2}+(\frac{\lambda}{10}-\lambda)^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$   BP = $\sqrt{\frac{9\lambda^{2}}{100}+\frac{81\lambda^{2}}{100}}$

= BP = $\sqrt{\frac{90\lambda^{2}}{100}}$

Now, PA = $\sqrt{(\frac{\lambda}{3}-\frac{3\lambda}{10})^{2}+(0-\frac{\lambda}{10})^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ PA = $\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{2}}{900}+\frac{\lambda^{2}}{100}} \Rightarrow PA$ = $\sqrt{\frac{10\lambda^{2}}{900}}$

Therefore BP : PA = 9 : 1

questions.question_html: A straight line through a fixed point (2, 3) intersects the coordinate axes at distinct points P and Q. If O is the origin and the rectangle OPRQ is completed, then the locus of R is :
questions.explanation_text: Let coordinate of point R = (h, k). Equation of line PQ, (y $-$ 3) = m (x $-$ 2). Put y = 0 to get coordinate of point p, 0 $-$ 3 = (x $-$ 2) $\Rightarrow$ x = 2 $-$ $\frac{3}{m}$ $\therefore$ p = (2 $-$ $\frac{3}{m}$ , 0) As p = (h, 0) then h = 2 $-$ $\frac{3}{m}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{3}{m}$ = 2 $-$ h $\Rightarrow$ m = $\frac{3}{2-ℎ}$ . . . . . . (1) Put x = 0 to get coordinate of point Q, y $-$ 3 $=$ m (0 $-$ 2) $\Rightarrow$ y = 3 $-$ 2m $\therefore$ point Q = (0, 3 $-$ 2m) And From the graph you can see Q = (0, k). $\therefore$ k = 3 $-$ 2m $\Rightarrow$ m = $\frac{3-k}{2}$ . . . . (2) By comparing (1) and (2) get $\frac{3}{2-ℎ}=\frac{3-k}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ (2 $-$ h)(3 $-$ k) = 6 $\Rightarrow$ 6 $-$ 3h $-$ 2K + hk = 6 $\Rightarrow$ 3 h + 2K = hk $\therefore$ locus of point R is 3x + 2y= xy
questions.explanation_html:
Let coordinate of point R = (h, k).

Equation of line PQ,

(y $-$ 3) = m (x $-$ 2).

Put y = 0 to get coordinate of point p,

0 $-$ 3 = (x $-$ 2)

$\Rightarrow$ x = 2 $-$ $\frac{3}{m}$

$\therefore$ p = (2 $-$ $\frac{3}{m}$ , 0)

As p = (h, 0) then

h = 2 $-$ $\frac{3}{m}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{3}{m}$ = 2 $-$ h

$\Rightarrow$ m = $\frac{3}{2-ℎ}$ . . . . . . (1)

Put x = 0 to get coordinate of point Q,

y $-$ 3 $=$ m (0 $-$ 2)

$\Rightarrow$ y = 3 $-$ 2m

$\therefore$ point Q = (0, 3 $-$ 2m)

And From the graph you can see Q = (0, k).

$\therefore$ k = 3 $-$ 2m

$\Rightarrow$ m = $\frac{3-k}{2}$ . . . . (2)

By comparing (1) and (2) get

$\frac{3}{2-ℎ}=\frac{3-k}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ (2 $-$ h)(3 $-$ k) = 6

$\Rightarrow$ 6 $-$ 3h $-$ 2K + hk = 6

$\Rightarrow$ 3 h + 2K = hk

$\therefore$ locus of point R is 3x + 2y= xy

questions.question_text: The sides of a rhombus ABCD are parallel to the lines, x $-$ y + 2 = 0 and 7x $-$ y + 3 = 0. If the diagonals of the rhombus intersect P(1, 2) and the vertex A (different from the origin) is on the y-axis, then the coordinate of A is :
questions.question_html: The sides of a rhombus ABCD are parallel to the lines, x $-$ y + 2 = 0 and 7x $-$ y + 3 = 0. If the diagonals of the rhombus intersect P(1, 2) and the vertex A (different from the origin) is on the y-axis, then the coordinate of A is :
questions.explanation_text: Let the coordinate A be (0, c) Equations of the given lines are x $-$ y + 2 = 0 and 7x $-$ y + 3 = 0 We know that the diagonals of the rhombus will be parallel to the angle bisectors of the two given lines; y = x + 2 and y = 7x + 3 $\therefore$ equation of angle bisectors is given as : $\frac{x-y+2}{\sqrt{2}}= \pm \frac{7x-y+3}{5\sqrt{2}}$ 5x $-$ 5y + 10 = $\pm$ (7x $-$ y + 3) $\therefore$ Parallel equations of the diagonals are 2x + 4y $-$ 7 = 0 and 12x $-$ 6y + 13 = 0 $\therefore$ slopes of diagonals are $\frac{-1}{2}$ and 2. Now, slope of the diagonal from A(0, c) and passing through P(1, 2) is (2 $-$ c) $\therefore$ 2 $-$ c = 2 $\Rightarrow$ c = 0 (not possible) $\therefore$ 2 $-$ c = $\frac{-1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ c = $\frac{5}{2}$ $\therefore$ Coordinate of A is $\frac{5}{2}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Let the coordinate A be (0, c)

Equations of the given lines are

x $-$ y + 2 = 0 and 7x $-$ y + 3 = 0

We know that the diagonals of the rhombus will be parallel to the angle bisectors of the two given lines; y = x + 2 and y = 7x + 3

$\therefore$ equation of angle bisectors is given as :

$\frac{x-y+2}{\sqrt{2}}= \pm \frac{7x-y+3}{5\sqrt{2}}$

5x $-$ 5y + 10 = $\pm$ (7x $-$ y + 3)

$\therefore$ Parallel equations of the diagonals are 2x + 4y $-$ 7 = 0

and 12x $-$ 6y + 13 = 0

$\therefore$ slopes of diagonals are $\frac{-1}{2}$ and 2.

Now, slope of the diagonal from A(0, c) and passing through P(1, 2) is (2 $-$ c)

$\therefore$ 2 $-$ c = 2 $\Rightarrow$  c = 0 (not possible)

$\therefore$ 2 $-$ c = $\frac{-1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ c = $\frac{5}{2}$

$\therefore$ Coordinate of A is $\frac{5}{2}$ .

questions.question_text: Let k be an integer such that the triangle with vertices (k, – 3k), (5, k) and (–k, 2) has area 28 sq. units. Then the orthocentre of this triangle is at the point :
questions.question_html: Let k be an integer such that the triangle with vertices (k, – 3k), (5, k) and (–k, 2) has area 28 sq. units. Then the orthocentre of this triangle is at the point :
questions.explanation_text: Given, vertices of triangle are (k, – 3k), (5, k) and (–k, 2). $\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} k & -3k & 1 \\ 5 & k & 1 \\ -k & 2 & 1 \end{aligned}|= \pm 28$ $\Rightarrow$ k(k - 2) + 3k(5 + k) + 1(10 + k 2 ) = $\pm$ 56 $\Rightarrow$ 5k 2 + 13k + 10 = $\pm$ 56 $\Rightarrow$ 5k 2 + 13k - 66 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ k = $\frac{-13 \pm \sqrt{-1151}}{10}$ So no real solution exist. or 5k 2 + 13k - 46 = 0 $\therefore$ k = $\frac{-23}{5}$ or k = 2 since k is an integer $\therefore$ k = 2 Thus, the coordinate of vertices of triangle are A(2, -6), B(5, 2) and C(-2, 2). Now, equation of altitude from vertex A is y - (-6) = $\frac{-1}{(\frac{2-2}{-2-5})}(x-2)$ $\Rightarrow$ x = 2 .......(1) Equation of altitude from vertex B is y - 2 = $\frac{-1}{(\frac{2+6}{-2-2})}(x-5)$ $\Rightarrow$ 2y - 4 = x - 5 $\Rightarrow$ x - 2y = 1 .......(2) Point H( $\alpha$ , $\beta$ ) lies on both (1) and (2), $\therefore$ $\alpha$ = 2 .........(3) $\alpha$ - 2 $\beta$ = 1 ......(4) Solving (3) and (4), we get $\alpha$ = 2 , $\beta$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore$ Orthocentre is $(2,\frac{1}{2})$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given, vertices of triangle are (k, – 3k), (5, k) and (–k, 2).

$\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} k & -3k & 1 \\ 5 & k & 1 \\ -k & 2 & 1 \end{aligned}|= \pm 28$

$\Rightarrow$ k(k - 2) + 3k(5 + k) + 1(10 + k2) = $\pm$ 56

$\Rightarrow$ 5k2 + 13k + 10 = $\pm$ 56

$\Rightarrow$ 5k2 + 13k - 66 = 0

$\Rightarrow$ k = $\frac{-13 \pm \sqrt{-1151}}{10}$

So no real solution exist.

or 5k2 + 13k - 46 = 0

$\therefore$ k = $\frac{-23}{5}$ or k = 2

since k is an integer $\therefore$ k = 2

Thus, the coordinate of vertices of triangle are

A(2, -6), B(5, 2) and C(-2, 2).



Now, equation of altitude from vertex A is

y - (-6) = $\frac{-1}{(\frac{2-2}{-2-5})}(x-2)$

$\Rightarrow$ x = 2 .......(1)

Equation of altitude from vertex B is

y - 2 = $\frac{-1}{(\frac{2+6}{-2-2})}(x-5)$

$\Rightarrow$ 2y - 4 = x - 5

$\Rightarrow$ x - 2y = 1 .......(2)

Point H( $\alpha$ , $\beta$ ) lies on both (1) and (2),

$\therefore$ $\alpha$ = 2 .........(3)

$\alpha$ - 2 $\beta$ = 1 ......(4)

Solving (3) and (4), we get

$\alpha$ = 2 , $\beta$ = $\frac{1}{2}$

$\therefore$ Orthocentre is $(2,\frac{1}{2})$ .

questions.question_html: Two sides of a rhombus are along the lines, $x-y+1=0$ and $7x-y-5=0$ . If its diagonals intersect at $(-1,-2)$ , then which one of the following is a vertex of this rhombus?
questions.explanation_text: Let other two sides of rhombus are $x-y+\lambda=0$ and $7x-y+\mu=0$ then $O$ is equidistant from $AB$ and $DC$ and from $AD$ and $BC$ $\therefore$ $|-1+2+1|=|-1+2+\lambda| \Rightarrow \lambda=-3$ and $|-7+2-5|=|-7+2+\mu| \Rightarrow \mu=15$ $\therefore$ Other two sides are $x-y-3=0$ and $7x-y+15=0$ On solving the equations of sides pairwise, we get the vertices as $(\frac{1}{3},\frac{-8}{3}),(1,2),(\frac{-7}{3},\frac{-4}{3}),(-3,-6)$

questions.question_text: Let $PS$ be the median of the triangle with vertices $P(2,2)$ , $Q(6,-1)$ and $R(7,3)$ . The equation of the line passing through $(1,-1)$ band parallel to PS is :
questions.question_html: Let $PS$ be the median of the triangle with vertices $P(2,2)$ , $Q(6,-1)$ and $R(7,3)$ . The equation of the line passing through $(1,-1)$ band parallel to PS is :
questions.explanation_text: Let $P,Q,R,$ be the vertices of $\Delta PQR$ Since $PS$ is the median, $S$ is mid-point of $QR$ So, $S=(\frac{7+6}{2},\frac{3-1}{2})=(\frac{13}{2},1)$ Now, slope of $PS$ $=\frac{2-1}{2-\frac{13}{2}}=-\frac{2}{9}$ Since, required line is parallel to $PS$ therefore slope of required line $=$ slope of $PS$ Now, equation of line passing through $(1,-1)$ and having slope $-\frac{2}{9}$ is $y-(-1)=-\frac{2}{9}(x-1)$ $9y+9=-2x+2$ $\Rightarrow 2x+9y+7=0$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $P,Q,R,$ be the vertices of $\Delta PQR$



Since $PS$ is the median, $S$ is mid-point of $QR$

So, $S=(\frac{7+6}{2},\frac{3-1}{2})=(\frac{13}{2},1)$

Now, slope of $PS$ $=\frac{2-1}{2-\frac{13}{2}}=-\frac{2}{9}$

Since, required line is parallel to $PS$ therefore slope of required line $=$ slope of $PS$

Now, equation of line passing through $(1,-1)$ and having slope $-\frac{2}{9}$ is

$y-(-1)=-\frac{2}{9}(x-1)$

$9y+9=-2x+2$

$\Rightarrow 2x+9y+7=0$

questions.question_text: A ray of light along $x+\sqrt{3}y=\sqrt{3}$ gets reflected upon reaching $X$ -axis, the equation of the reflected ray is :
questions.question_html: A ray of light along $x+\sqrt{3}y=\sqrt{3}$ gets reflected upon reaching $X$ -axis, the equation of the reflected ray is :
questions.explanation_text: $x+\sqrt{3}y=\sqrt{3}$ or $y=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}x+1$ Let $\theta$ be the angle which the line makes with the positive x-axis. $\therefore$ $tan\theta=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=tan(\pi-\frac{\pi}{6})$ or $\theta=\pi-\frac{\pi}{6}$ $\therefore$ $\angleABC=\frac{\pi}{6}$ ; $\therefore$ $\angleDBE=\frac{\pi}{6}$ $\therefore$ the equation of the line BD is, $y=tan\frac{\pi}{6}x+c$ or $y=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}+c$ ..... (1) The line $x+\sqrt{3}y=\sqrt{3}$ intersects the x-axis at $B(\sqrt{3},0)$ and, the line (1) passes through $B(\sqrt{3},0)$ . $\therefore$ $0=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}+c$ or, c = $-$ 1 Hence, the equation of the reflected ray is, $y=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}-1$ or $y\sqrt{3}=x-\sqrt{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
$x+\sqrt{3}y=\sqrt{3}$ or $y=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}x+1$

Let $\theta$ be the angle which the line makes with the positive x-axis.

$\therefore$ $tan\theta=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=tan(\pi-\frac{\pi}{6})$ or $\theta=\pi-\frac{\pi}{6}$

$\therefore$ $\angleABC=\frac{\pi}{6}$ ; $\therefore$ $\angleDBE=\frac{\pi}{6}$

$\therefore$ the equation of the line BD is,

$y=tan\frac{\pi}{6}x+c$ or $y=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}+c$ ..... (1)

The line $x+\sqrt{3}y=\sqrt{3}$ intersects the x-axis at $B(\sqrt{3},0)$ and, the line (1) passes through $B(\sqrt{3},0)$ .

$\therefore$ $0=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}+c$ or, c = $-$ 1

Hence, the equation of the reflected ray is,

$y=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}-1$ or $y\sqrt{3}=x-\sqrt{3}$

questions.explanation_text: The line passing through the intersection of lines $ax+2by=3b=0$ and $bx-2ay-3a=0$ is $ax+2by+3b+\lambda(bx-2ay-3a)=0$ $\Rightarrow (a+b\lambda)x+(2b-2a\lambda)y+3b-3\lambda a=0$ As this line is parallel to $x$ -axis. $\therefore$ $a+b\lambda=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=-a/b$ $\Rightarrow ax+2by+3b-\frac{a}{b}(bx-2ay-3a)=0$ $\Rightarrow ax+2by+3b-ax+\frac{2a^{2}}{b}y+\frac{3a^{2}}{b}=0$ $y(2b+\frac{2a^{2}}{b})+3b+\frac{3a^{2}}{b}=0$ $y(\frac{2b^{2}+2a^{2}}{b})=-(\frac{3b^{2}+3a^{2}}{b})$ $y=\frac{-3(a^{2}+b^{2})}{2(b^{2}+a^{2})}=\frac{-3}{2}$ So it is $3/2$ units below $x$ -axis.
questions.explanation_html:
The line passing through the intersection of lines

$ax+2by=3b=0$

and $bx-2ay-3a=0$ is

$\Rightarrow (a+b\lambda)x+(2b-2a\lambda)y+3b-3\lambda a=0$

As this line is parallel to $x$ -axis.

$\therefore$ $a+b\lambda=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=-a/b$

$\Rightarrow ax+2by+3b-\frac{a}{b}(bx-2ay-3a)=0$

$\Rightarrow ax+2by+3b-ax+\frac{2a^{2}}{b}y+\frac{3a^{2}}{b}=0$

$y(2b+\frac{2a^{2}}{b})+3b+\frac{3a^{2}}{b}=0$

$y(\frac{2b^{2}+2a^{2}}{b})=-(\frac{3b^{2}+3a^{2}}{b})$

$y=\frac{-3(a^{2}+b^{2})}{2(b^{2}+a^{2})}=\frac{-3}{2}$

So it is $3/2$ units below $x$ -axis.

questions.question_text: A square of side a lies above the $x$ -axis and has one vertex at the origin. The side passing through the origin makes an angle $\alpha(0<\alpha<\frac{\pi}{4})$ with the positive direction of x-axis. The equation of its diagonal not passing through the origin is :
questions.question_html: A square of side a lies above the $x$ -axis and has one vertex at the origin. The side passing through the origin makes an angle $\alpha(0<\alpha<\frac{\pi}{4})$ with the positive direction of x-axis. The equation of its diagonal not passing through the origin is :
questions.explanation_text: Co-ordinate of $A=(acos\alpha,asin\alpha)$ Equation of $OB,$ $y=tan(\frac{\pi}{4}+\alpha)x$ $CA\perp^{r}$ to $OB$ $\therefore$ slope of $CA=-$ $cot(\frac{\pi}{4}+\alpha)$ Equation of $CA$ $y-asin\alpha=-cot(\frac{\pi}{4}+\alpha)(x-acos\alpha)$ $\Rightarrow (y-asin\alpha)(tan(\frac{\pi}{4}+\alpha))=(acos\alpha-x)$ $\Rightarrow (y-asin\alpha)(\frac{tan\frac{\pi}{4}+tan\alpha}{1-tan\frac{\pi}{4}tan\alpha})(acos\alpha-x)$ $\Rightarrow (y-asin\alpha)(1+tan\alpha)=(acos\alpha-x)(1-tan\alpha)$ $\Rightarrow (y-asin\alpha)(cos\alpha+sin\alpha)=(acos\alpha-x)(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)$ $\Rightarrow y(cos+sin\alpha)-asin\alpha cos\alpha-asin^{2}\alpha$ $=acos^{2}\alpha-acos\alpha sin\alpha-x(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)$ $\Rightarrow y(cos\alpha+sin\alpha)+x(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)=a$ $y(sin\alpha+cos\alpha)+x(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)=a.$
questions.explanation_html:
Co-ordinate of $A=(acos\alpha,asin\alpha)$

Equation of $OB,$

$y=tan(\frac{\pi}{4}+\alpha)x$

$CA\perp^{r}$ to $OB$

$\therefore$ slope of $CA=-$ $cot(\frac{\pi}{4}+\alpha)$

Equation of $CA$

$y-asin\alpha=-cot(\frac{\pi}{4}+\alpha)(x-acos\alpha)$

$\Rightarrow (y-asin\alpha)(tan(\frac{\pi}{4}+\alpha))=(acos\alpha-x)$

$\Rightarrow (y-asin\alpha)(\frac{tan\frac{\pi}{4}+tan\alpha}{1-tan\frac{\pi}{4}tan\alpha})(acos\alpha-x)$

$\Rightarrow (y-asin\alpha)(1+tan\alpha)=(acos\alpha-x)(1-tan\alpha)$

$\Rightarrow (y-asin\alpha)(cos\alpha+sin\alpha)=(acos\alpha-x)(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)$

$\Rightarrow y(cos+sin\alpha)-asin\alpha cos\alpha-asin^{2}\alpha$

$=acos^{2}\alpha-acos\alpha sin\alpha-x(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)$

$\Rightarrow y(cos\alpha+sin\alpha)+x(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)=a$

$y(sin\alpha+cos\alpha)+x(cos\alpha-sin\alpha)=a.$

questions.explanation_text: Equation of $AB$ is $xcos\alpha+ysin\alpha=p;$ $\Rightarrow \frac{xcos\alpha}{p}+\frac{ysin\alpha}{p}=1;$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x}{p/cos\alpha}+\frac{y}{p/sin\alpha}=1$ So co-ordinates of $A$ and $B$ are $(\frac{p}{cos\alpha},0)$ and $(0,\frac{p}{sin\alpha});$ So coordinates of midpoint of $AB$ are $(\frac{p}{2cos\alpha},\frac{p}{2sin\alpha})=(x_{1},y_{1})(let);$ $x_{1}=\frac{p}{2cos\alpha}&y_{1}=\frac{p}{2sin\alpha};$ $\Rightarrow cos\alpha=p/2x_{1}$ and $sin\alpha=p/2y_{1};$ $cos^{2}\alpha+sin^{2}\alpha=1 \Rightarrow \frac{p^{2}}{4}(\frac{1}{x_{1}^{2}}+\frac{1}{y_{1}^{2}})=1$ Locus of $(x_{1},y_{1})$ is $\frac{1}{x^{2}}+\frac{1}{y^{2}}=\frac{4}{p^{2}}.$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of $AB$ is

$xcos\alpha+ysin\alpha=p;$

$\Rightarrow \frac{xcos\alpha}{p}+\frac{ysin\alpha}{p}=1;$

$\Rightarrow \frac{x}{p/cos\alpha}+\frac{y}{p/sin\alpha}=1$

So co-ordinates of $A$ and $B$ are

$(\frac{p}{cos\alpha},0)$ and $(0,\frac{p}{sin\alpha});$

So coordinates of midpoint of $AB$ are

$(\frac{p}{2cos\alpha},\frac{p}{2sin\alpha})=(x_{1},y_{1})(let);$

$x_{1}=\frac{p}{2cos\alpha}&y_{1}=\frac{p}{2sin\alpha};$

$\Rightarrow cos\alpha=p/2x_{1}$ and $sin\alpha=p/2y_{1};$

$cos^{2}\alpha+sin^{2}\alpha=1 \Rightarrow \frac{p^{2}}{4}(\frac{1}{x_{1}^{2}}+\frac{1}{y_{1}^{2}})=1$

Locus of $(x_{1},y_{1})$ is $\frac{1}{x^{2}}+\frac{1}{y^{2}}=\frac{4}{p^{2}}.$
